bio.en: Farhan Thawar is Vice President and Head of Engineering at Shopify, where he helps run a 10,000-person fully-remote engineering organization known for its urgency, velocity, and first-principles thinking.
bio.zh: Farhan Thawar 是 Shopify 的工程副总裁兼工程负责人，管理着一支 1 万人、完全远程的工程组织，该组织以紧迫感、高速执行和第一性原理式的思考著称。

summary.en: Farhan shares concrete tactics for maintaining intensity and urgency at scale, including unusual meeting cadences, a constant drive to delete code (their 'Delete Code Club'), and the counterintuitive power of pair programming. He advocates 'creating intensity' by doing more per minute rather than more hours, and explains why he defaults to the harder option when choosing between paths because it ultimately makes life easier. He also offers sharp hiring advice—including how Shopify plans to bring on over a thousand engineering interns—and reflects on a career of working alongside a different billionaire each decade.
summary.zh: Farhan 分享了在规模化下保持强度与紧迫感的具体做法，包括独特的会议节奏、持续删代码的“删代码俱乐部”，以及结对编程那种反直觉的力量。他主张通过“每分钟做更多”而非“工时更长”来制造强度，并解释为何在两个选项之间他默认选择更难的那条路，因为它最终让人生更轻松。他还给出了犀利的招聘建议——包括 Shopify 计划招募上千名工程实习生，并回顾了自己“每十年换一位亿万富翁老板”的职业生涯。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: If you do the hard path and it doesn't work, actually you still win because you've now done something hard. You've probably worked with smart people. You've learned something along the way that is valuable. I meet lots of job seekers. I go, what are you doing to try to find a job? Are you really learning anything from sending out 10 resumes a day? Why don't you look at the API Docs and build something? Even if you don't get a job at Shopify, you've learned something.
turns.zh: 假如你选择了艰难的道路却未能成功，实际上你依然是赢家——因为你已挑战了自我极限。或许你曾与才华横溢之人共事，在此过程中收获了宝贵的成长经验。我接触过许多求职者，当我问他们：“你采取了哪些有效的求职策略？”他们往往回答：“我每天投递十份简历，真能学到什么吗？” 何不去研究API文档并开发些小项目呢？即便未能在Shopify获得职位，你也将收获专业技能。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: First, I want to talk about another theme, creating intensity in your organization.
turns.zh: 接下来，我想谈谈组织中营造紧迫感的另一个主题。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Everyone says, "Oh yeah, work hard and do more hours when you're young, whatever." I'm like, "What if you just did more per minute?"
turns.zh: 人们总说：“年轻时多加班、多付出总没错。” 但我更想问：“若你能把每分钟的工作效率提升呢？”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The more I dig into the Shopify way working, the more fun stuff I never expected emerges. There's been a drive to delete code and simplify.
turns.zh: 越深入了解Shopify的工作方式，就越能发现许多意想不到的创新之处。比如，团队始终致力于代码精简与架构优化。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: We have a Delete Code Club. We can always almost find a million-plus lines of code to delete, which is insane.
turns.zh: 我们专门成立了“删除代码俱乐部”，每次都能删除数百万行冗余代码，效率令人惊叹。

turns.zh: 我曾读到你的一句话：“不是每个人都能在公众面前反复出丑，但我认为这就是我的超能力。”

turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Advice that I've heard you share with people often is when they're trying to decide amongst a bunch of options is to choose the harder path because that makes life easier down the road. Share this advice why it's so important, where you learned, where you developed that this is the right approach.
turns.zh: 我经常听到你给人们的建议是，当他们在众多选项中犹豫不决时，应该选择更困难的道路，因为这会让未来的生活更加轻松。请分享一下这个建议为何如此重要，你是从哪里学到的，又是在哪里形成这种正确方法的。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: But the short version is that if you have a choice and you choose the easy thing and it works great. If you choose the hard thing and it works great, you did more work, but if it doesn't work and you chose the easy thing, you've actually not learned anything because you chose the... You haven't done a lot of work, you haven't probably worked with the smartest people because they're not usually around on the easy path, and what happens is you've gone through this exercise and now you're like, I've kind of lost. I lost the choice, or I was trying to do something, it didn't work out for me. But if you do the hard path and it doesn't work, actually you still win because you've now done something hard. You've probably worked with smart people, you've learned something along the way that is valuable, and I can give you a quick example. (00:06:41): So I meet lots of job seekers and they're like, I go, "What are you doing to try to find a job?" I'm like, "I'm sending out 10 resumes a day." I'm like, "Okay." That sounds kind of easy, and are you really learning anything from sending out 10 resumes a day? Versus I would say to them, "Hey, you know all these companies you're interested in, Shopify might be one of them. Why don't you look at the API Docs and build something, build a Shopify app, build an admin extension, build something on top of Shopify." Even if you don't get a job at Shopify, which is maybe your goal, you've learned something, you've built something, you have things in your GitHub repo now and you can show people. You're learning about the product that might translate to a job you might get somewhere else. So I think that even though it's harder, right? Of course, you can't every day build an app on a different platform. (00:07:23): Maybe you can once a day. You will learn something in the hard path. And the same thing happened to me in taking hard courses. I would get worse marks, but I ended up meeting smarter people in those courses because they were there for the same reason I was because the content was hard. And so that's something that I've just realized in my life that if I do the hard thing and I just naturally tend towards doing that, I ended up doing... I went to Waterloo and I did a minor in electrical engineering on top of computer science, and when I did my MBA, I did a minor in financial engineering because the smarter people were in that path and they're still my friends today.
turns.zh: 简而言之，如果你有选择的机会，选择了简单的方式且效果显著，那自然没问题。但如果你选择了困难的路径，效果同样出色，那固然值得，但如果结果不理想，那就说明你没有真正学到什么东西——因为你选择了简单之路，就意味着你没有与最优秀的人共事，而这些人才往往不会出现在简单路径上。当你经历了这个过程后，可能会觉得自己迷失了方向，失去了选择的机会，或者努力的方向失败了。但如果你选择了困难的路径，即便结果不尽如人意，你依然能从中收获宝贵的经验。我可以举个例子：（00:06:41）我经常遇到求职者，他们会说：“我在找工作，每天发送10份简历。”我会问：“你对感兴趣的公司，比如Shopify，有了解吗？”他们会说：“有啊。”这听起来挺简单，但每天发送10份简历真的能学到什么吗？相比之下，我会建议他们：“嘿，你对Shopify感兴趣，那为什么不看看API文档，开发个Shopify应用、管理后台扩展，或者基于Shopify平台做些开发呢？”即便你最终没能在Shopify找到工作（这或许是你的初衷），你也能积累经验，掌握新技能，GitHub仓库里有可展示的成果，还能将这些技能应用到其他工作中。所以，虽然困难，但坚持下去总是值得的。当然，你不可能每天都在不同平台开发应用，但或许每天尝试一个新项目也未尝不可。在困难的学习过程中，同样的道理也适用。我成绩可能不算出色，但在那些课程中我结识了更聪明的人，因为他们和我一样选择了挑战。这些经历让我意识到，如果我坚持做难事，最终总能有所收获。比如我在滑铁卢大学攻读计算机科学时，同时修读了电气工程辅修课程；读MBA时，我选择了金融工程辅修，因为那里汇聚了更多优秀人才，他们至今仍是我的良师益友。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So building on the last point you just made, people could hear this and think, okay, if it's harder, that's going to be the right path. Sometimes harder is still a bad idea. For example, joining a terrible company that's extremely frustrating to work at or building, I don't know, a house in a really dumb way, but it's just really hard. What else do you find is important to think about when you're thinking it's not just harder, but also XYZ should probably be true?
turns.zh: 回到你刚才提到的观点，人们可能会听了觉得，既然困难，那就应该选择困难的路径。但有时困难的选择也未必明智。比如加入一家糟糕的公司，工作极其痛苦；或者用愚蠢的方式建房子，虽然费力但结果不佳。当你认为某件事既困难又有价值时，还需要考虑哪些其他因素？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, one real one is of course the people, because I find that my path has always focused on trying to pick the best learning journey. Where can I learn the most? And for me, everyone's different. Some people might learn better from books or the domain they're in, but for me, I learn a lot from people, and so I try to put myself in those harder rooms on purpose. There was a time when I was doing my MBA in financial engineering, by the way, and I'm a tech guy and still a tech guy, and all these people were going into finance jobs. (00:08:46): There was a point where somebody said to me, "Why are you in this class?" Because they knew that I was doing it for fun, and so it was because it was the learning journey. And so I would say a big part of it for me is yes, there's the how do you win even if you lose, because if it goes poorly, you can still come out of it with skills, but if you actually take the hard path, you'll have these intense working relationships with smart people that again will continue on in your life. (00:09:12): And that also just forces you to be in this constant state of uncomfort by going into these rooms and saying, "I don't know anything," and it's harder. And I agree with you. You don't want to do dumb things like, oh, let's just do this thing in a dumb way. That's not what I mean. I mean, let's try to do the hard thing that we can learn from. And by the way, it happens to be on the path. It's just is it might take more manual work or it might not be the way most people do it, but we think we can learn more from that path.
turns.zh: 是的，真正重要的人当然是其他人。我发现我的职业生涯始终致力于选择最优质的学习之路。在哪里能学到最多知识？对每个人来说答案各不相同。有些人可能更擅长从书本或所在领域中学习，但对我而言，我从与人交流中获益良多。因此，我会刻意选择更具挑战性的环境。说起来，我攻读金融工程硕士学位时就是这种情况——毕竟我本质上还是个技术人员，但周围所有人都一心想进入金融行业。（00:08:46）：当时有人问我：“你为什么来上这门课？”因为他们知道我只是为了兴趣而来，所以这门课对我而言就是一场学习之旅。我想说，对我而言，关键在于即使失败也要如何取胜。即便事情进展不顺利，你也能从中获得技能。但如果你选择更艰难的道路，你将与聪明人建立深厚的工作关系，这些关系会伴随你一生。（00:09:12）：这种选择也意味着你必须不断处于不舒适的状态——走进这些房间时说：“我什么都不懂。”这确实更难。但我同意你的观点——你不想做愚蠢的事，比如“我们就用这种愚蠢的方法吧”。这不是我的意思。我是说，让我们尝试那些能让我们学到更多知识的困难之路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Speaking of that, I found this great quote from you, "Not everyone can look stupid in public over and over, but I believe it's my superpower and I try to make it my whole team's superpower too."
turns.zh: 说到这里，我发现你曾说过一句很棒的话：“不是每个人都能在公众面前一次又一次地出丑，但我相信这是我的超能力，我也试图让整个团队拥有这种能力。”

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, it sounds funny, but again, I'm the one who's always trying super dumb things and sometimes they work, and even my wife hates that I try these things even at home, right? I'll just like, what's an example? It might be a new washing machine and I might try some weird mode with some clothes, and I'm like, "Oh, you ruin the clothes." I'm like, okay. But now I know that this mode should not be used, but maybe I would've uncovered that there's some super fast, quick wash that I can do in 20 minutes that now saves us 40 minutes of wash time every single time we use the washing machine. (00:10:22): So there's things like that, but I will ruin lots of clothes trying to do that, but the same at work. We'll try things and sometimes it can lead to disaster, hopefully not, but you can imagine people trying to like, oh, let me try this new configuration of GCP and maybe we'll get some benefit, but maybe we'll take Shopify down. We don't want to do that. So you want to have some sort of guardrails. But there is something around trying dumb things and saying dumb things. Half the time, by the way, when I say something dumb, people go, "I had the same question." They just were scared to say it.
turns.zh: 是啊，这听起来挺搞笑的，但说真的，我总是尝试一些超级愚蠢的做法，有时还能成功，就连我妻子都讨厌我在家也这样尝试。比如，买台新洗衣机时，我可能会尝试一些奇怪的模式，结果衣服被毁了。我只能说好吧。但现在我知道这种模式不能用，或许我还能发现一种20分钟就能洗好的快速模式，这样每次用洗衣机时就能节省40分钟的洗涤时间。（00:10:22）：类似这样的例子还有很多，但为了尝试这些方法，我确实毁了不少衣服。工作中也是如此。我们会尝试新东西，有时可能会导致灾难性后果，但愿不会。不过你能想象人们会尝试新配置的GCP，结果可能导致Shopify宕机。我们可不想这样。所以你需要设定一些防范措施。但尝试愚蠢想法、说出愚蠢话语的过程中，也确实能收获不少。顺便说一句，当我说出蠢话时，很多人会说：“我也曾有过同样的疑问。”他们只是害怕说出来。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So for folks that may want to, because I feel like this skill is so hard, but so important, being okay with failing, being okay with looking dumb, is there something you tell people to help them build this other than just like, I'm genetically good at this stuff? What helped you become comfortable with being wrong and failing before you were a big shot exec where it's like, oh, he's fine. He knows what he's doing.
turns.zh: 所以对于那些可能想学习的人——因为我觉得这种技能既难又重要——如何接受失败，如何坦然面对出丑，有没有什么秘诀？除了天生就擅长这些技能之外，你还做了哪些努力，才能在成为大公司高管之前，就能坦然面对错误和失败？比如，现在人们会说：“他没事，他很清楚自己在做什么。”

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: I don't know. I mean, I kind of grew up working in retail and people come into the store, and then I would say, "Hey," and you're working on commission, and they're not always buying stuff, and if they don't buy it, you don't make any money. And so maybe just the fact of going up and forcing myself to talk to people and then trying to get them to, and maybe you spend an hour with a client and then they don't buy anything, but you're getting that reaction of a bunch of negatives, and all you have to do is say, okay, and just go to the next customer. You can't really well on it and be like, oh my God, my whole day is ruined. But instead, you have to learn from that and say, "Okay, let me try this. Let me try that." And it's not easy, but it was a way to build up some confidence and people say, this telemarketing, or there's a bunch of things you can do to get a lot of rejection. Cold calling is another one, and that can lead you to actually building up resistance. I don't know if I'm genetically better at it or not. I just think that I literally don't care if I look dumb. I've always said the dumb thing, I'm not doing things on purpose to get nos, which by the way, is part of some sales training, which is go and get 10 nos. But I haven't done that. But I have been in many situations with many sharp people, business people, successful people who have said to me... Turn around and said, "That's the stupidest fucking question I've ever heard." I've definitely had that happen to me. And I'm like, "All right, let's move on to the next question."
turns.zh: 我不知道。我是说，我在零售业工作长大，每当有人进店时，我会说声“嘿”，然后你靠佣金提成挣钱，但他们不总是会买东西。如果他们不买，你就赚不到钱。所以也许最难的部分就是主动上前跟人搭话，然后努力促成交易。可能你会花一个小时跟客户交流，结果他们什么也没买，但你得到的全是负面反馈。你只能调整心态，说：“好吧，再试试下一个客户。”你不能因此情绪崩溃，觉得自己一天都毁了。相反，你要从中吸取教训，说：“好，我试试这个，再试试那个。”这并不容易，但确实能帮助你建立自信。人们常说电话营销很困难，或者说很多事情都会遭遇大量拒绝。冷电话销售也是如此，可能会让你产生抗拒心理。我不知道自己是否天生更擅长这类事。我只觉得自己不在乎显得愚蠢。我总是说些蠢话，也不是故意去招惹别人拒绝。顺便说一句，有些销售培训会教你先去找10个拒绝你的人。但我从没这么做过。不过我确实遇到过很多精明的商界人士，他们对我说："这是我听过最蠢的问题了。"这种情况确实发生过。我就说："好吧，那我们换个问题吧。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that attitude and I think that's key to it. It's just bounce off of it and not be crumble and I think it's empowering for folks to hear from someone like you that has done so well that people tell you that is the dumbest question I've ever heard-
turns.zh: 我喜欢这种态度，我觉得这才是关键。就是从容应对，不被击垮。我觉得听你这样成功人士说这些话，对听众很有启发——

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Oh yeah, still.
turns.zh: 哦，对啊，还是这样。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Still. Okay.
turns.zh: 还是这样。好吧。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah. So how about this? That I heard that's the dumbest fucking question. And then recently I heard, I've already explained this to you three times because I kept asking and I didn't understand, and literally I got this message back saying, "I've already explained this to you three times." I'm like, "Okay, I still don't get it." So my goal there is not to annoy the person, but it's to understand the content. And actually, by the way, I say these were messages, I saved them. I literally screenshot it because I'm like, remember this? It doesn't matter. I'm trying to learn.
turns.zh: 是啊。所以你怎么看？比如说，我听过别人说这是最蠢的问题。最近我又听到有人说："我已经给你解释三次了，因为你老是问却不明白。"我说："好吧，可我还是不明白。"所以我的目标不是惹人烦，而是理解内容。顺便说一句，我保存了这些消息，还截了图，因为我想，记住这点很重要。无所谓，我只是想学习。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: One more question along these lines. I was looking at your LinkedIn and your career history, and I noticed that you worked for a different billionaire every decade of your life. So there's a guy named Joe Lemond in your twenties and Chamath in your thirties and Toby this decade, maybe yourself next decade, if things go well. Other than what you've shared or maybe it is what you've shared, is there a thread across these three folks that have been really successful that you've learned from that maybe is consistent across them all or even just specific to each one?
turns.zh: 再问一个相关的问题。我看你的领英和职业经历，发现你每十年都会为不同亿万富翁工作过。二十多岁时是乔·勒蒙德，三十多岁是查马特，这十年是托比，也许下个十年是你自己，如果一切顺利的话。除了你分享的经历，或者说正是你分享的经历之外，这三位非常成功的人身上有没有共通之处？你能从他们身上学到什么？是所有人共通的，还是各自独有？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: It's interesting because again, this is looking back, you're like, wait a sec, I didn't plan it this way. There's no way you could plan it, right? I'm going to work for a different billionaire every decade. That's not how it works but they're similar. They're mostly different people, but they're similar in one thing is that they have an irrational view of what the world should look like over the next decade or so. They're very long-term thinkers, very rational in that they'll look and say, "Hey, in 10, 15, 20, 25 years, this is what the world's going to look like." And I'm not good at seeing that vision, but I'm good at trying to move towards that vision 1% a week. And so the melding of the two, I know where I'm good and I'm good at pushing the ball forward. And if they're good at the long-term vision, we can both align to say, "You're good at this thing. I'm good at this thing. Why don't we merge forces?" (00:14:35): And so that is something that has resonated with me is like, how do I find these irrational all progress depends on the unreasonable man. How do I pair with these people because I'm altogether too reasonable and there's no way for me to become unreasonable, and so I have to merge with these people. And so that is again, something that I specifically have sought out. And even when I was starting my own company in 2015, I actually sat down and wrote a list of all the unreasonable people that I knew in Toronto, and I went down the list and met every single one of these entrepreneurs to figure out are we API compatible and could I work with them? And I ended up picking one of them and starting a company.
turns.zh:
这一点很有意思，因为回过头来看，你会发现，等等，我可没这么打算过。这种事根本没法提前规划，对吧？我每十年就会为不同的亿万富翁工作一次。这听起来不现实，但他们其实有相似之处。他们大多是不同的人，但有一点相似之处是，他们对未来十年的世界应该是什么样子有着不切实际的看法。他们是长远主义者，非常理性，他们会审视未来10年、15年、20年、25年的世界模样。我不擅长构想那种愿景，但我擅长每周朝着那个愿景前进1%。所以两者的结合，我知道自己的强项所在，我善于推动事情向前发展。如果他们擅长长远规划，我们就能携手合作，说：“你擅长这个，我擅长那个。我们为何不携手共进呢？”（00:14:35）  
所以让我深有共鸣的是，我该如何找到这些不切实际的人？一切进步都依赖于不合常理的人。如何与这些人合作呢？因为我太过理性，根本无法变得不理性，所以我必须与他们合力。所以这也是我特意去寻找的。甚至在2015年创办自己的公司时，我还专门列了一个清单，写下我在多伦多认识的所有不合常理的人，然后逐一拜访这些创业者，探讨我们是否能在API层面兼容，能否合作。最终我选中了其中一人，共同创办了公司。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is an amazing story. So first of all, I just love this insight that being aware of this is not a superpower of mine and I'm not going to try to build it. I'm going to find someone to merge with, and connect your APIs together and be the person that builds it, not the person that envisions what to build. I think that's awesome because a lot of people... I need to get good at all these things. I need to become the best at vision and strategy and execution and collaboration and then all these things. And so I think alone, this isn't really interesting instead it's just recognize your strengths and weaknesses and double down on your strengths.
turns.zh: 这真是个了不起的故事。首先，我很欣赏这种洞察力——承认这不是我的超能力，我不会去刻意培养它。我会去寻找能与我合力的人，连接彼此的API，充当那个落地者，而不是空想家。我觉得这很棒，因为很多人……我需要在所有这些方面都变得出色。我需要成为最擅长愿景、战略、执行、协作等各方面的人。而单枪匹马，这其实没什么意思，关键在于认识自己的长处和短处，然后在长处上加倍努力。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, it sounds funny, but me and you talked about it that a framework I wrote down, which I tweet out, me writing that down changed how I picked jobs forever, right? Because I had this lull after my first job in between where I was trying to figure out why nothing felt as exciting as my first job. And it turns out that it took me to sit down and be like, what do I actually care about? And people can get confused. I get confused all the time, by the way, by things that are not on my framework. So for example, a good one, title, company, money, all these things can confuse you because you could have somebody say recruiter messages you and says, "Hey, by the way, here's a new job and here's the compensation." You're like, "Oh my God, this is exciting." And if you don't have a written down framework of the things you actually care about, it's very hard to be distracted. So very hard not to be distracted. You get distracted by that. So instead, I look at the framework and go, does this align with my framework? Right? (00:16:43): Actually to the point of, I actually sent my framework to a recruiter one time and I said, "Hey, this thing," because they kept going back and forth to me and I go, "Hey, this doesn't align with my framework." So it really saves me time from not being distracted, but it also forced me to think about every year I can reevaluate what I'm doing and look at the framework and say, "Is this true to my values?" Now, my wife will say this, that I'm like a robot. When I realize that my framework is being violated, I will resign instantly and I've done that before. So without even having another job or anything, I just go like, oh, my framework is being violated and then resign. There's this thing where I know what I enjoy working on, and that framework helps me find it. And so I encourage everyone, anybody looking for a job I always say, "Write down a framework. You can use mine as inspiration, but figure out what you care about and make sure that what you're working on lines up with that."
turns.zh: 是啊，这听起来挺有趣的，但我和你之前聊过，我写下来的那个框架，我在推特上分享过。写下那个框架彻底改变了我找工作的思路，对吧？因为我在第一份工作结束后，经历了一段迷茫期，总觉得没有什么工作能比得上第一份工作那么令人兴奋。后来我意识到，必须静下心来问自己：我真正在乎的是什么？人们可能会被各种因素迷惑。比如，职位头衔、公司名声、薪资待遇，这些都会让人分心。如果有人给你发招聘信息，说：“嘿，顺便说一下，这里有个新职位和对应的薪资。”你可能会兴奋不已。但如果你没有写下来的核心价值观框架，就很难抵御这种干扰。说真的，我有次甚至把自己的框架发给招聘人员，说：“嘿，这个职位不符合我的框架。”这样既节省了被干扰的时间，又能每年重新评估自己的选择，审视框架，问自己：“这些价值观是否依然真实？”我妻子会说，我就像个机器人。一旦发现框架被违背，我会立即辞职。我以前就这么做过。甚至不找下家，就因为框架被破坏了。这个框架能让我明确自己喜欢做什么工作，也能帮助我找到理想职位。所以我鼓励所有找工作的人：写下自己的框架，可以参考我的示例，但要明确自己在乎什么，确保工作内容与价值观相符。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this framework is the questions to ask about where to go work. That's your framework. Okay, cool. We'll link to that so folks can check it out. The example of you resigning when it didn't meet your framework, is that a story you're up for sharing? Is there something to learn from that?
turns.zh: 这个框架就是用来指导求职方向的。好的，很棒。我们会附上链接，方便大家参考。你辞职的例子能分享一下吗？从中能学到什么经验？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, sure. So this happened when I was at my previous, a few companies ago, we were running a mobile company called Xtreme Labs. That was the one that Chamath was the major investor in and so we worked with him directly. And what I realized was... And so that company was amazing. We worked on it for many years. It was a mobile app development company. We got to work on mobile apps for the biggest brands in the world, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, Vine, the NFL, NBA, Bloomberg, Slack, you name it we worked on those mobile apps, and this is right when the iPhone and Android were really gaining steam in '09 to 2013 era. And then we eventually got acquired by Pivotal. And over time, my role at Pivotal, Pivotal, and Pivotal Labs changed from, hey, I was running the biggest office in the world. I was running the biggest pair programming office. (00:18:34): I'm a big fan of pair programming to one in which we were really trying to attach consulting to the product. And I ended up being a field CTO, which really, I mean it was fun to learn about that world, but it was different than what I was doing. And so if I looked across my framework, it was violating all the things that I was trying to work. I wasn't working with the smartest people anymore. I was on IC. I wasn't learning as much as I could be learning. And so I wasn't on this and I wasn't having a lot of impact. I was like, oh, wait a sec, this is completely not aligned. And then I just told the team, "Hey, I plan on resigning." And that, by the way, led to great other things because I'm an investor in new companies that have spun out from there and it was a great experience. I'm just saying it at the time, lended me to say, "Hey, you're not actually focused on the right things."
turns.zh: 是啊，当然了。这事发生在我之前任职的几家公司之一，当时我们运营着一家名为Xtreme Labs的移动公司。查马斯（Chamath）是该公司的主要投资者，所以我们直接与他合作。我意识到……那家公司非常出色。我们为它投入了多年心血。这是一家移动应用开发公司，我们曾为全球顶级品牌开发移动应用，比如Facebook、Twitter、Instagram、Vine、NFL、NBA、彭博社、Slack等等，只要你能叫得出名字的，我们都为其开发过移动应用。正值2009至2013年间，iPhone和安卓系统势头正盛之际。后来我们被Pivotal收购了。随着时间推移，我在Pivotal的角色发生了转变——最初我负责管理全球最大的办公场所，运营最大的结对编程团队。（00:18:34）我非常推崇结对编程，但后来我们开始尝试将咨询服务与产品开发相结合。最终我成为了一名现场CTO，坦白说，我很享受了解那个领域的乐趣，但这与我之前的工作截然不同。回顾我的职业框架，我发现自己违背了所有努力方向。我不再与最顶尖的人才共事，而是处于独立承包状态，无法充分学习新知识。因此，我的贡献微乎其微。我意识到，天啊，这完全不符合我的价值观。于是我直接对团队说：“嘿，我打算辞职了。” 顺便说一句，这次选择带来了丰厚回报，因为我投资了从那里衍生出来的新公司，这是一段美好的经历。我当时只是想说，‘嘿，你们并没有专注于正确的事情。’

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to come back to Xtreme Labs. I know there's other stories there that are interesting, but first I want to talk about another theme of things that people often raised when I asked them about you. And this one is intensity, and it's specifically creating intensity in your organization and the value of that, the power of that. I've seen that the way you describe this and I love is how do you expend more kilojoules per hour versus spend more hours on work. So talk about just why intensity, first of all, is so important to an organization.
turns.zh: 我想再谈谈Xtreme Labs。我知道还有其他有趣的故事，但首先我想探讨另一个主题——当我询问人们对你的看法时，他们经常提及的一个主题。那就是“专注力”，以及在组织中创造专注力的重要性及其价值。我注意到你对此的描述，我很欣赏你提出的观点：如何在单位时间内输出更多价值，而非单纯延长工作时长。首先，请谈谈为什么专注力对组织如此重要。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah. So I think there's a few things. One, I have this fundamental belief that one hour is one hour. It's the same hour. If you spend an hour or I spend an hour, it's the same time that goes by. And if I just expend more calories in that hour. Let's say we both work nine to five. If I can just get more done in the nine-to-five, we have both... The time has elapsed the same for us, but I just got more done. And that allows me, of course, then I'd be like, "Hey, I'm going to take my kid to soccer and do other stuff." We can still do the same things out of work, but during work, I just want to try to get as much done as possible during the time versus expanding the time and I can give you an example. I used to work at a company where it was like I worked 12 hours a day, but I was playing foosball in the middle of the day. (00:20:37): And then we'd go for a coffee break and you do these things. And of course, the time expanded to 12 hours versus trying to compress into that eight-hour day. And pair programming is a great example because, so it's such an intense activity. Two people on one machine, you can get so much done when two people are working together, not being distracted by the internet and distractions, and just focus on writing the solution to the problem at hand. And it's so tiring that usually when people switch on to pair programming, they sleep 10 to 12 hours a night the first few nights because it's so intense. You're working so hard. But for me, that intensity actually leads to extraordinary outcomes even if you don't have to put in more hours. I think most people, you probably hear this all the time, everyone says, "Oh yeah, work hard and do more hours when you're young, whatever." (00:21:26): I'm like, what if you just did more per minute? Like quickly get through things. I think there's another unintuitive fact is that people who are really good can actually output high-quality collateral quickly. So take a person who is good and extremely good, the extremely good person can actually get a lot of output in a short amount of time, and the person who's good might take longer. I think there's a time variance there that people don't think about. So you can not drop the quality too much, but get the time down by 2X, 3X, right? Parkinson's Law of scale instead of, if I give you an hour to do something, a really good person can get a high-quality output in one hour.
turns.zh: 是的。我认为有几个关键点。首先，我坚信一小时就是一小时。时间是固定的，无论你还是我，每个小时流逝的时间都是一样的。如果我能在这一个小时内完成更多工作——假设我们都朝九晚五上下班——那么虽然我们的时间消耗相同，但我却能完成更多任务。这样一来，我就可以腾出时间去做其他事情，比如带孩子去踢足球。下班后我们依然可以做自己想做的事，但在工作时间里，我只想尽可能高效地完成任务，而不是把时间拉长。我可以举个例子。我曾在一家公司工作，虽然每天工作12小时，但中午我会玩桌上足球，休息时间也各种摸鱼。当然，时间就这样被拉长到了12小时，而不是专注于如何在8小时内完成更多工作。对程式设计而言，结对编程就是一个很好的例子。两个程序员共用一台电脑，专注于解决手头的问题，不受网络和其他干扰影响，效率极高。但这种高强度工作通常会让人筋疲力尽，刚开始转向结对编程时，很多人前几晚都会睡10到12个小时，因为实在太累了。但对我而言，这种高强度反而能带来非凡的成果，即便不需要投入更多时间。我想大多数人可能都听过这种说法：“年轻时多努力工作，多加班，等等”。（00:21:26）但我更想说，如果能提高每分钟的效率呢？比如快速完成任务。我还发现一个反直觉的现象：真正优秀的人能够快速产出高质量的成果。以两种水平的人为例，优秀的人能在短时间内完成大量工作，普通人则需要更长时间。这是人们通常忽视的时间差异。只要不牺牲质量，把时间缩短2倍、3倍，难道不香吗？这就是帕金森定律的反面——不是说“给一小时做事”，优秀的人能在一小时内产出高质量的成果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I want to talk about how you create an org that operates this way, but specifically, you just mentioned pair programming. I know that's one of your favorite tools. Talk about why this is so powerful when you recommended... I think as an outside observer, it's like two engineers on the same code. Why wouldn't we do things half as fast? Talk about just why you're a big fan of pair programming specifically.
turns.zh: 我还想谈谈如何打造一个以这种方式运作的组织，但具体来说，你刚刚提到了结对编程。我知道这是你最喜欢的工具之一。能否谈谈为什么它如此有效？作为局外人来看，就是两个工程师共同编写同一段代码。为什么他们不会工作得更慢呢？能否具体说说你为何如此推崇结对编程？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: It is the most underutilized management tool in engineering, bar none. It is just not used as much as it could be. So pair programming, for those who don't know, it's two people on one computer. So two keyboards, two mics, two monitors, but one computer, they work together and if it's remote, they use it. You can use a tool like tuple, which we use, and you can just remotely be on one computer, and you're totally right. The famous tweet about pair programming is, wait a sec, we have two engineers on one computer, won't they write half as much code? And the answer is, oh, no, no, they'll write even less than that because it's not about lines of code. The throughput limiter is not hands-on keyboard. It's not like we're both sitting there and the limiter is like us trying to get through the keystrokes onto the screen. (00:23:12): The limiter is where is the good elegant solution? How do we think through the problem and build the right solution for the problem at hand? Tobi famously built a lot of Shopify paired programming, and what he would do is he would actually set a timer and him and the CTO Cody would pair program for one hour. And if they did not finish the problem in one hour, they would delete all the code and they would keep the tests and they would start over. And then what their thinking was, if we were not able to articulate and write the code for this feature in one hour, we must be on the wrong design. We must be building the wrong thing and so they delete all the code, kept the tests, and then wrote it again. And sometimes he'd be over by one minute and he would still delete the code and start over because his thinking was the right elegant solution should be able to be written in one hour. (00:24:03): And so pair programming, I mean, that's an extreme version of it, but even at Pivotal Labs, if your pair was sick that day and you wrote a bunch of code, the strong version is your pair would come in the next day, delete all the code that you wrote, and then you'd write it again the next day. And again, what better time to rewrite code than right after you've written it because you now know the problem domain? And by the way, it sounds like a waste of time. It sounds like I'm just deleting code but the reason is that code lives a long time. Code is a liability and the right solution, the usually shorter lines, more elegant solution tends to appear after you've done a bunch of pathfinding. And the only way to do that pathfinding is start and then delete and then start and be like, oh, no. (00:24:47): Now I know. Delete. And it's super hard to delete, by the way, because we're humans and we have this sunk cost fallacy, so it's hard to delete. But if you can do that, you will actually land upon a much, much better solution. And of course, pair programming has high, high rates of learning because you're just sitting beside... You're not only whether it's tuple or remote or directly, you learn keystrokes and you learn how somebody thinks about a problem. You go back and forth on the talking, and yes, you will write probably less code, but you will move faster along the path of delivering value for your customers than you would if you did it on your own. And there's all these studies that show happiness is higher, knowledge transfer is higher, less silos, intensity is higher, all the things. And at a price of 20% or something of what you would normally do. (00:25:33): The analogy I have is the underhanded free throw in basketball, statistically known to sink more baskets, but looks dumb and nobody does it. Literally, Shaquille O'Neal, I'm not that big a basketball fan, but I read this about Shaquille O'Neal, who's a Hall of Famer, and they said, "Why don't you throw underhand?" Because he was notoriously bad at free throws and he goes, "It looks dumb." Even though he's paid millions of dollars a year to do this thing. It looks dumb, doesn't want to do it.
turns.zh:
它是工程领域最被低估的管理工具，无人能及。只是人们没有充分利用它。那么，什么是结对编程呢？对于不熟悉的人来说，就是两人共用一台电脑。也就是说，两套键盘、两个麦克风、两块显示器，但只用一台电脑。他们协同工作，若是远程合作，就可以通过工具如Tuple（我们使用的平台）实现远程共享一台电脑。没错，结对编程的核心不在于敲多少代码，而在于如何高效解决问题。著名的结对编程案例是Shopify的Tobi和CTO Cody，他们会设定一小时的编程时限，若一小时内未完成任务，就会删除所有代码，保留测试从头再来。他们的逻辑是：如果一个功能的代码在一小时内写不出来，那说明设计有问题，我们必须重新构思方案。（00:23:12）

结对编程的极端版本是，Tobi曾与CTO Cody在一小时内完成某个功能的编程，若未达成目标，他们就会删除所有代码，保留测试重头再来。Pivotal Labs也有类似做法：若结对伙伴生病，编写的代码会被删除，次日重新编写。（00:24:03）

结对编程看似浪费时间，但删除代码实则有深意。代码是沉没成本，重写代码能让问题更清晰。（00:24:47）

结对编程极大促进学习：通过实时交流，双方不仅能掌握编码技巧，更能领悟对方的思维方式。（00:25:33）

结对编程成本仅为传统开发的20%，但带来诸多益处：提升幸福感、知识共享、消除隔阂、提高效率等。
奥尼尔，我对篮球不是很感兴趣，但我读到过关于名人堂成员沙奎尔·奥尼尔的报道，他们问他：“你为什么不尝试用手臂下方投篮？”因为他在罚球方面出了名的糟糕，而他回答说：“那看起来很蠢。”尽管他每年能赚数百万美元做这份工作，但他就是觉得那动作太难看了，根本不想尝试。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I remember those Shaquille O'Neal years when he had a special free throw coach, and I remember them talking about this-
turns.zh: 我记得沙克·奥尼尔效力湖人队的那些年，他有专门的罚球教练。我还记得人们谈论这件事时——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... When he hit a special free throw coach. And, I remember them talking about this and he's like, "No, I'm never going to do that."
turns.zh: ……当他成功投中一记特别的罚球时。我记得他们谈论此事时，他说"不，我永远不会那样做。"

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: "I'm never going to do it." Because it looks dumb. And by the way, go back to the beginning of the interview. I don't care what looks dumb or looking stupid, we're going to do this. And so, actually, I ran the biggest pair programming shop in the world.
turns.zh: "我永远不会那么做。"因为那看起来很傻。顺便说一句，回到采访开头。我不在乎什么看起来傻或显得愚蠢，我们要坚持下去。所以实际上，我曾运营过全球最大的结对编程团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: On that note, so what percentage of shop Shopify do this? Is this how y'all operate?
turns.zh: 说到这，Shopify团队中有多少人采用这种方式？这是你们的运营模式吗？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah. So, Shopify, I mentioned that Toby and Cody did this at the beginning of Shopify. And the cool thing about pair programming is, and in my old world at XtremeLabs is that we knew exactly what to build, because we were building mobile apps that were almost like contract manufacturing. We're like, "We have an iOS version. Can we build an Android version?" So, we quickly were able to say, "Here's the spec. Go quick." Shopify is such a different company, right? We are a pathfinding company. We are trying to find the right thing to build. And so, pair programming may or may not make sense all the time. Like Pivotal and Xtreme, we were doing 40 hours a week. (00:26:54): Shopify is much more of a four to eight hour a week pair programming culture, where you're gathering together on a problem and saying, "Hey, let's pair for half a day, or let's pair every Wednesday." And we use that tool in our arsenal to move quickly down a path. But a lot of other time is spent pathfinding and trying to figure out what to build, and trying to convince field be like, "Hey, we're going to go down this path. Oh, now I know exactly." (00:27:16): And sometimes, by the way, 18 months later, we've now figured out all the things and that's the time we should delete everything and start over. And, that's something that we will do at that point. And so, you don't want to be pair programming for 18 months. You want to be wayfinding and pathfinding. And then go, "I see the matrix. Let me just delete everything and now build it." Because the learning is what you're going for. We have all the learning, now let's write the code.
turns.zh: 是的。Shopify早期，我提到托比和科迪就这么做了。结对编程的妙处在于，在XtremeLabs的旧团队中，我们清楚要开发什么产品，因为我们开发的移动应用几乎像合同制造一样。我们会说：“我们有iOS版本，能不能开发安卓版本？”所以我们能迅速说：“这是规格说明，快去开发。”Shopify则完全不同，对吧？我们是一家开拓性公司，不断探索正确的开发方向。因此，结对编程未必总是适用。在Pivotal和XtremeLabs时期，我们每周投入40小时。（00:26:54）：Shopify则更倾向于每周4到8小时的结对编程文化，大家聚在一起解决问题，说：“嘿，结对编程半天吧，或者每周三都结对。”我们用这种工具快速推进开发。但大部分时间都在探索方向、确定要开发的内容，并说服团队：“嘿，我们要走这条路了。哦，现在我完全清楚了。”（00:27:16）：顺便说一句，有时18个月后，我们才搞清楚所有问题，这时我们就该删掉所有代码重新开始了。到那时，我们才会那么做。所以你不会想结对编程18个月。你需要探索和开拓方向，然后说：“我看清了全局，删掉所有代码，重新开始吧。”因为学习才是关键。我们已经掌握了知识，现在就去写代码。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Got it. So it's basically, when the code, you're pretty sure this is correct and it's really important segments of the code base pair program.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以基本上，在代码特别重要且复杂的部分，你们会选择结对编程。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah. And then also we do a lot of pairing during an incident or a way to figure out together, work with somebody and say, "Hey, I'm not really sure and let's jump on a call together or jump on a tuple and go down the path." And say, "Let's figure out together what's going on."
turns.zh: 是的。此外，我们在遇到问题时也会经常结对编程，比如一起分析问题、与同事沟通说：“嘿，我不太确定，让我们开个电话会议或用Slack一起解决。”然后一起理清思路。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I can't help but ask AI, how does that impact this way of working?
turns.zh: 我不禁想问AI，这对这种工作方式有什么影响？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: So, AI is super interesting. What's happening right now with an AI copilot like GitHub Copilot is it is your pair programmer. So, you now can feel like you're pairing actually without another human. You can pair with the AI. And so, what's happening too is that you're seeing people use Whisper, like they're talking to Cursor, and they're talking through Whisper to say, "Okay, let's build a new React component that does this." And they're talking and then it's building. "Oh no, that's not what I meant. I meant doing this." So you can actually not even have to type, just using voice, go back and forth with your pair programmer. (00:28:35): I would say, that's amazing. I would still contend take that experience and add two humans together. So you've got an AI copilot and humans, because what's happening is generating code. And the two humans can look and say, "Oh, I know what it's trying to do." And, either delete the code, because you have inspiration and write it yourself, or just take the suggestion and move it forward. But, I love today's world of AI copilots, because you never have to code loan on your own right? You never have to code alone. You can try a different language now, because the API and the syntax is much easier to pull forward. And so, all of those things are a win for engineering and a win for everybody who wants to build any software.
turns.zh:
嗯，人工智能确实非常有趣。目前像GitHub Copilot这样的AI副驾驶功能，它就像你的编程搭档。现在你甚至无需面对面合作就能感受到这种协作体验——你可以和AI进行编程对话。比如，用户会使用Whisper平台，就好像在和Cursor对话一样，通过Whisper平台发出指令，比如“好的，我们来构建一个新的React组件来实现这个功能。”然后AI会根据指令进行代码生成。用户可能会说：“不对，我不是这个意思，我是想这样做。”这样一来，你甚至无需动手敲代码，只需通过语音与AI进行交流即可。

（00:28:35）我觉得这太棒了。但我还是更倾向于让两个人一起合作——一个AI副驾驶和一个真人程序员。毕竟编程本质上是代码生成的过程。两个人可以一起审视代码，说：“哦，我明白它的意图了。”然后要么删除代码，发挥自己的创意重新编写，要么采纳AI的建议继续推进。但我真的很喜欢当今的AI副驾驶技术，因为你再也不用独自编程了。现在你可以尝试不同的语言，因为API和语法都变得更易于上手了。总之，这对工程师和所有想要开发软件的人来说都是一大利好。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That makes a lot of sense. Basically, everyone's going to be a pair programmer-
turns.zh: 这说得很有道理。基本上每个人都会成为编程搭档——

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 是的，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... In the future. Okay, I want to come back to what else you have done at Shopify to create intensity. And I think, again, it's important to highlight the intensity is meant to, "How do we get more done in the time we have and then go home?" Not just work all day every day, weekends kind of intensity.
turns.zh: ……在未来。好的，我想再回过头来谈谈你在Shopify为提升工作效率所做的其他努力。我觉得，再次强调，提升效率的核心在于“如何在有限的时间内完成更多工作，之后再回家？”而不是每天从早到晚埋头工作，周末也无休止地加班。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah. So we have a few things that we have going for us, right? So one, we have this tool called GSD, which stands for get shit done, which you've probably heard from maybe talking to other Shopify folk, which is this notion of weekly updates to the whole company on what's happening. Again, Parkinson's law at scale. If you ask people every week, they want to show progress every single week. So that's one way I talked about pair programming as well. The other thing we do as a company is, we used to have twice a year was our cadence, Black Friday, Cyber Monday, or we had an event in the summer. And now, we do six-week reviews. So, teams have this notion of every six weeks actually coming together and walking through the roadmap, the resourcing, and what they're working on with their immediate leadership, but then also, with Toby. (00:30:18): And so, what's cool about that, and by the way, it's a huge time investment, right? We all get into a room, it's happening tomorrow. So Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, a bunch of us will be in the office together and we're going to go through every project in the company, and we're going to talk about the project, the resourcing, how it's going, and we're going to make changes. And again, that creates intensity, because you want to show what has been done, what have you learned since the last six-week review. And, we find six weeks is a very good cadence, because it's short enough that you can remember the context and it's long enough... Six weeks is long enough, especially if you have, let's say, a team of a dozen engineers, you can do a lot. And not only that, you can do a lot in a day, but this is a check-in point. (00:30:59): And what I've noticed too with intensity is, let's say, we get a review and there's some feedback we get in that review. We don't wait until the next six-week review, right? The next day we are building things, we are iterating, we are tagging people. And then, by the next week's we're like, "Here's the trajectory." Right? Actually, I want to get that Elon shirt made, "What have you done this week?" Because, Parkinson's law is real. It sounds funny, but I keep bringing this up, but whatever time you allot to something will be the time it takes, right? (00:31:26): So, if you're doing something monumental, I don't know, you're doing a reorg or something, right? You can do it the slow way. "Let's sit down, and plan, and roll it out." And it's probably six months in most companies. Shopify, this is a week or two. You sit down, you're like, "Hey, this is the bones of it. Let's bring some more people and think." But then, it's going to start leaking. So we just launch it. Right? And, we do the same thing with lots of things. We just try to move more quickly and get out of the... We don't do change management, we just land it, and then go, "Hey everyone, it's a volatile company. This is what's happening. But this is how we get things done quickly." And then, move on with our lives.
turns.zh:
是啊。所以我们有几个有利因素，对吧？首先，我们有一个叫GSD的工具，全称是Get Shit Done（把事情做完），你们可能听其他Shopify员工提过。这是一种每周向全公司汇报进展的机制。这其实就是帕金森定律在大规模应用——如果你每周都问大家进展如何，他们就会想每周都展示成果。

另外，我们公司还推行了六周评审机制。过去每年有两次大型活动，分别是黑五和网一，现在改成了每六周一次。每个团队每六周都会聚在一起，回顾路线图、资源配置和当前进展，同时与直属领导和托比一起讨论。（00:30:18）这种方式很棒，但投入巨大——明天（周二、周三、周四）我们会召集所有人，花一天时间逐一审查每个项目，讨论进展、资源配置和改进方向。这能激发团队热情，因为大家要展示成果、分享经验，及时调整计划。六周周期恰到好处——既短到能清晰记忆上下文，又长到能完成大量工作。

（00:30:59）我还发现，高强度推进机制很有效。比如评审后收到反馈，我们不会等到下次六周评审才行动。第二天就能开始迭代、分配任务。到下周，我们就能汇报进展：“这是当前路径。”对吧？比如我要把那件埃隆马斯克主题T恤做出来，问“这周做了什么？” 因为帕金森定律真实存在。听起来很搞笑，但我一直强调——你分配给某件事的时间，往往就是它完成所需的时间。

（00:31:26）比如大规模重组？没错，你可以慢慢来——“坐下来规划，再逐步实施”，但大多数公司要花六个月。我们只需一两周。先定框架，再集思广益，然后迅速上线。我们在很多事上都这样操作，快速推进，不搞变革管理，直接落地，然后告诉大家：“我们是高成长公司，变化不可避免，但我们认为快速行动更重要。”然后继续前进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, there's so much there. I have been through the six-month reorgs. And, I think that context you just shared of, "We're at a volatile company, we're changing things. It's not going to be smooth, but we think this is for the best." It's just the culture of Shopify. It sounds like, "We want to keep moving fast. We know this isn't going to be the smoothest thing, but we just know this better to make the change at this point versus wait."
turns.zh: 哇，内容真多。我经历过六个月的重组过程。你们刚才提到的“我们是高成长公司，正在变革，过程不顺利，但这是正确的选择”，这就是Shopify的文化。听起来像是“我们要保持快速前进，知道这不会一帆风顺，但我们认为此刻变革比等待更重要”。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: It's how Toby increased the resiliency in the company. He would walk around in the old days when we had a data center and just unplugged machines, right?
turns.zh: 这就是托比如何提升公司的韧性的。过去我们有数据中心的时候，他会四处走动，直接拔掉机器的电源，对吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Chaos monkey.
turns.zh: "混沌猴"。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, chaos monkey. You're right. But that actually works, because it just says, "Hey, by the way, shit's going to break. And so, let's be resilient to that." And so, same thing here. "Hey, by the way, someone's going to move your cheese. It's fine. We are here to create more entrepreneurs in the world. We're not here to have a six-month change management roadmap. And, that will just actually hurt the speed at which we can deliver value to merchants."
turns.zh: 对啊，“混沌猴”。你说得没错。但这招确实有效，因为它就是在告诉大家：“嘿，顺便说一句，系统可能会出故障。那么，让我们对此保持韧性。”这里道理也一样。“嘿，顺便说一句，总有人会来‘偷走你的奶酪’。不过没关系。我们来这儿是为了培养更多创业者，不是为了制定长达六个月的变革管理路线图。那样只会拖慢我们为商家创造价值的速度。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So, on all the things you shared, so there's weekly updates. So the weekly updates are each person shares what they're working on for the week. Is that the idea?
turns.zh: 所以，关于你提到的这些内容，每周都有更新。每周更新就是每个人分享自己当周的工作进展。对吧？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Each project.
turns.zh: 每个项目。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Each project.
turns.zh: 每个项目。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: So, each project, it has an update, it might have a video of, "Here's the experience." It'll have a obviously a bunch of writing on what's changed since last time. We have a process called OK1 and OK2, which is like, OK1 is typically at the director level where they're like, "Okay, I'm aligned with the direction that this is going at." Or, "I'm not aligned." And they can make changes. Then, when it goes to OK2, it's typically the VP level of the area, who's now looking to say, "Okay. What you're working on actually aligns with the overall architecture. But by the way, have you looked at this context? Maybe you haven't seen this, this is happening, or the industry." And so, you're trying to align at that level. And then, again, like I mentioned, every six weeks we go through with Toby, and he's an intense guy himself. (00:33:40): And so, a lot of it is like, "Hey, why is this taking so long? Are we overthinking it? Are we not trying to move forward on this thing, because we're blocked on something? Is there some piece of infra?" Actually, I'll give you a good example. In one of the reviews from last time, there was an interesting AI problem we were trying to solve with LLMs that required us to have a very large output context window. And, most of the LLMs today have a very small output context window. But in the review, right, we have shared Slack channels with all the LLM folks, right? I messaged in the open AI channel, I messaged in the Gemini channel, whatever. And, within an hour we had increased the context on a bunch of major models and we were able to move forward through the thing, just because I asked. (00:34:29): And so, that's an example. It didn't take another six week review, but it increased the intensity, because the team was like, "Oh, we were blocked because we thought we had to now chunk up this data and do this thing because we had smaller output context and we thought we could do a big input context, but we'd have to do this caching." And, it was like this whole thing. I'm like, "Well, did we just ask them if we get bigger?" And then, they were like, "Oh, we don't have this as undocumented, but we'll just enable it right now for Shopify." And so, that created the intensity of the team to be like, "Oh, we can now quickly get unblocked." So that's the example of just moving quick and trying to just, again, ask a dumb question. I'm like, "This is probably not possible, but..." And then, they came back and said, "Oh yeah, we can do that."
turns.zh:
因此，每个项目都会进行更新，可能会有一个视频，展示“项目进展情况”。显然，项目更新还包括对上次迭代后所做更改的详细说明。我们有一个名为OK1和OK2的流程。OK1通常由项目主管层级把控，他们会评估项目是否与既定方向一致，或者是否存在偏差，并进行必要调整。进入OK2阶段后，则由副总裁级别的人员负责审查，确保项目符合整体架构，同时兼顾行业背景和最新动态。

每六周，我们会与Toby（注：可能是指某位高管）进行评估，他是个要求严格的人。我们会反复追问：“为什么进展如此缓慢？我们是否过度思考？是否因某个技术瓶颈而停滞不前？是否存在基础设施层面的问题？”举个例子：在上次评审中，我们试图用LLM模型解决一个AI问题，需要设置非常大的输出上下文窗口。但目前大多数LLM模型的输出上下文窗口都很小。于是，我在公开的AI频道、Gemini频道等地方发消息询问，仅一小时内，就有多个主流模型成功提升了上下文窗口。这就是高效协作的典范——团队原本以为需要分割数据才能实现大规模输出上下文，但实际上只需启用相关功能即可。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a great example. And, as you're describing the ways that you create intensity and velocity within Shopify, it's interesting that what you're listing is a bunch of meetings and check ins, which to most people would feel like, "Why do we need so many..." There's all this like, "Less meetings." And I know you guys famously cancel all your meetings and that's a whole thing we can talk about. But, it's interesting that more check ins and regular check ins allow you to move faster. I imagine it's partly because it just makes sure you're not working on things that are unnecessary, and dumb, and not going to be used. And it's just continue to refine, these are actually the most important.
turns.zh: 这真是个绝佳的例子。虽然没有经历完整的六周评审周期，但通过紧急协调解决了问题，效率极高。因为团队意识到，之前的技术瓶颈源于误以为必须将数据分割成小块才能处理大规模输入上下文，却忽略了现有模型支持更大上下文的功能。通过直接启用该功能，团队得以快速突破技术壁垒。这充分说明，关键在于提出看似愚蠢的问题："有没有可能实现？"而对方给出肯定答复时，团队就能迅速行动。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: I mean, it's a combination of trust but verify, right? Because don't forget, the goal of the check-in is not for you to be like, "Ha, ha, I caught you not doing your work." It's not like the Dilbert boss, "Hey, did you do your thing?" Right? Even when I look at the Elon text, which is like, "Hey, what did you get done this week?" It wasn't to try to catch Parag in a, "You didn't do anything or you did a bunch of useless stuff." It was hopefully to pair on the problem, meaning, when I ask somebody, "Hey, did we move forward on this LLM project, because we now have this larger context window?" And then, they came back and said, "Oh, here's what we learned." So then, I can then look at the answer and say, "Oh, so now, have you thought of this? Have you tried..." It's a way to pair on the problem. (00:36:18): So, we have this word, everybody talks about micromanagement as a word, and we don't actually think it's a dirty word at Shopify, but the reason we don't think it's a dirty word is because it's not just, again, Dilbert boss saying, "Where did you do the thing?" It's like, "Hey, can I work on this problem with you? And if I work on this problem with you, I got to see where you are pretty often, and then give you advice, or you're going to share context with me, because I'm not in the work every day." To then come back and say, "Oh, based on what I know and what you know, can we move this in this direction? Maybe that's better for merchants." (00:36:50): I don't want to overuse the pairing paradigm, but it is really much like, "Can I pair with you?" And I learned this actually very early in my Shopify tenure, because Toby would have these one-on-ones with me and I'd be like, "Toby, you don't have to waste your time, man. You hired me. I got this." Well, he goes, "Oh, you misunderstand why you're here. We are here to work on problems together." And I was like, "Oh, I didn't even think..." I thought he hired me to take problems away. He hired me to work on problems with me. That's completely different than what I thought.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这是一种"信任但要核实"的组合，对吧？因为别忘了，开会的目的不是让你得意洋洋地说："哈，哈，我抓到你没做工作了。"这可不是《呆伯特》里老板那样的态度，"嘿，你今天做了什么事了？"对吧？就连埃隆发的那条短信，"嘿，这周你完成了什么？"也不是为了抓帕拉格没做事或者做了些无用功。希望是能一起解决问题——比如，当我问某人："嘿，我们在LLM项目上有没有进展？因为现在我们有了更大的上下文窗口。"然后他们回复："哦，我们总结了这些经验。"这样我就能看他们的回答，接着说："哦，那你有没有考虑过这个？有没有尝试过……"这就是一起解决问题的方式。（00:36:18）：所以，我们常提到微管理这个词，但在Shopify，我们并不认为这是个贬义词。之所以不认为它是贬义词，是因为这不只是《呆伯特》里老板那种"你今天做了什么事了？"的模式。而是像这样："嘿，我能和你一起解决这个问题吗？如果我和你一起解决这个问题，我得经常了解你的进展，然后给你建议，或者你得和我分享上下文，因为我没法每天参与工作。"然后再反馈说："哦，根据你我掌握的信息，我们能朝这个方向推进吗？也许对商家更友好些。"（00:36:50）：我不想过度使用"一起解决问题"这个模式，但它的本质确实是"我能和你一起解决问题吗？"我很早就在Shopify就学到了这一点，因为托比会和我开一对一会议，我当时会说："托比，你不用浪费时间的，伙计。你雇佣我来是让我解决问题的。"他却说："哦，你误解了你在这里的意义。我们是来一起解决问题的。"我当时就说："哦，我都没想到……"我以为他雇佣我是为了让我接手问题的。但他雇佣我是为了和我一起解决问题。这和我的想法完全不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. Okay. One thing you mentioned is meeting thing. For people that don't know what you all did with meetings, I think it might be worth just sharing that briefly, because it's awesome and something a lot of companies can learn from.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。好的。你提到的一个点是关于会议的。对于不了解你们会议模式的人来说，可能值得简单分享一下，因为这很棒，很多公司都能从中借鉴。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, sure. Actually, the funny story about the meeting Armageddon, is that, I was messaging Toby prior to me starting at Shopify about meeting Armageddon. And so, I actually think I had a little hand in him doing this before I got to Shopify. I was like, "Hey, have you seen..." I think it was Dropbox, "Have you seen a Dropbox is doing and Meetingageddon? And so, he was like, "This is super interesting." This is years before I started. So, I think it's funny that it ended up being a real thing. But here's what we do. Once a year at a random time, we will delete all recurring meetings that have more than two people, so not one-on- ones, and are internal people only, so not interviews or external partner meetings. And then, we have a two-week moratorium where you're not allowed to add a reoccurring meeting. You can have a regular meeting, but not a reoccurring meeting. (00:38:11): And the idea is that there's a lot of inertia behind a recurring meeting. It just always is there, and you know it's coming up, and it's hard to delete, because you're like, "Oh yeah, we talk about this thing every week." And so, what we do is we just do a meeting reset. And, I think, yeah, it's just called chaos monkey and the admins go in and just delete everything. Now what's cool about it is, it forces you to rethink, "Do we need a recurring meeting? Or do we just need one meeting? Or do we need a different cadence?" That's one thing. The other thing is it frees up so much crafter time, right? (00:38:42): One of the stats I track across engineering is how many hours are individual contributors in meetings per week? And we noticed that after we did... We did two things by the way. And I have a spicy second one for this, but the first one was we deleted meetings. And the second thing we did was we moved a lot of our Slack into Facebook workplace, which I'll talk about. Those are the only two things we did. And we saw a huge decrease in the amount of time crafters were in meetings. And then, we saw all kinds of other productivity enhancements, because they were able to have that flow time and work on things. (00:39:12): So, we're at something like three hours of meetings per week for an individual contributor at Shopify, which is phenomenal. Three hours a week is amazing. I think managers is not that bad. I think I tweeted this. I think it's six or seven hours per week. That's not bad at all, in order to get aligned. And then, all the rest of the time is work time.
turns.zh: 是的，当然了。其实关于“会议末日”（Meetingageddon）的趣事是，在我加入Shopify之前，我曾给托比发消息，提议开个会讨论这个项目。当时我觉得自己对他后来开展这个项目有点功劳。我当时说：“嘿，你看过Dropbox做的一个叫‘Meetingageddon’的项目吗？”他回答：“这太有意思了。” 这比我加入Shopify早好几年。所以现在想起来觉得挺巧的，结果它还真成了现实。不过我们现在的做法是，每年随机选个时间点，删除所有重复召开且参与人数超过两人的会议——不包括一对一会议，也不包括内部人员参加的会议，比如面试或外部合作伙伴会议。然后会有两周的禁令期，期间不允许添加任何重复召开的会议。可以开普通会议，但不能是重复召开的会议。（00:38:11）这样做的原因是，重复召开的会议背后有很强的惯性。它总是存在着，人们知道它即将到来，又很难删除，因为你会想：“哦对，我们每周都会讨论这个事。” 所以我们就通过这种方式重置会议安排。我觉得这叫“混沌猴子”策略，管理员会进去，直接把所有会议删掉。现在最酷的是，它能迫使人们重新思考：“我们真的需要重复召开的会议吗？还是只需要一次性会议？或者调整会议频率？”这是一方面。另一方面，它能释放出大量工作时间，对吧？（00:38:42）我追踪的工程部门数据之一是每个贡献者每周参加会议的时长。结果发现，在我们采取措施后——顺便说一下，我们做了两件事。第一件事是删除重复召开的会议。第二件事是把很多Slack聊天迁移到Facebook Workplace（我稍后会讲到）。这就是我们做的两件事。结果我们看到贡献者参加会议的时间大幅减少。随之而来的是各种生产力提升，因为他们能够专心工作了。（00:39:12）现在Shopify每个贡献者每周参加会议的时间大约是三个小时，这太棒了。三个小时太惊人了。我觉得经理们的会议时间也不算太糟。我记得我发过推特，说他们每周有六七个小时用于对齐工作。剩下的时间都是工作时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And how many hours was it before Meetingageddon and Workplace?
turns.zh: 那在“会议末日”和迁移到Workplace之前，会议时长是多少？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, you're asking me a good question. I have to go look and see. But, it came down by something like 50 or 60%. It was something like five or six hours for individual contributors and came down to three. And then, the managers, I think it was 10 that came down to 6, something like that. But it was a huge difference. And the only two things, like I mentioned, were one was the Meetingageddon, the other one was like this, and I can talk about this. This is a-
turns.zh: 是啊，你问了个好问题。我得去查一下。但减少了大概50%到60%。之前每个贡献者每周参加五六个小时的会议，现在降到了三个小时。经理们之前是10个小时，现在降到了6个小时左右。变化非常大。正如我提到的，就做了两件事，一是实施“会议末日”，二是迁移到Facebook Workplace。这些都是关键因素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yes, let's talk about this.
turns.zh: 是的，我们来聊聊这个吧。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: ... Yeah. So, I mean, I love Slack. It's the IM tool. Everybody uses it. But it can for sure cause distraction. And so, what we did was we moved all announcement information. So, anytime you're sending a status update or large group announcement, we moved all of that to Facebook Meta Workplace, like Facebook for work basically, which is now being deprecated. So, we'll have to figure that out. But, it just moved all this stuff to a ML feed that you can consume differently than you would Slack, because Slack is like I message you and you see an alert and all this stuff, versus Workplace is like, "Oh, I want to go and consume content from the company, and get updates, and share updates." And so, that reduced a lot of distraction as well. And so, I'd love to figure out what the next tool for us is, but it is probably something more like a river of information that I can dip my toe into, versus IM and chat everywhere.
turns.zh: 嗯……是的。我的意思是，我喜欢Slack。这是个即时通讯工具，大家都在用。但它确实容易让人分心。所以，我们把所有公告信息都转移了。比如，每当你发送状态更新或群组公告时，我们就把这些内容迁移到Facebook Workplace（基本上就是Facebook的企业版，不过现在这个平台正在逐渐退役）。所以，我们得另想办法。不过，这些信息都被移到了一个机器学习信息流里，用户使用体验和Slack有所不同。Slack是那种我给你发消息，你收到通知然后查看内容的模式，而Workplace则更像是“我想要去获取公司的信息、接收更新并分享动态”。这样大大减少了干扰源。我很想知道接下来我们该用什么工具，但很可能是那种能让我适度获取信息的平台，而不是到处都是即时通讯和聊天的地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is super interesting. So, specifically, things that are just updates where you don't need a discussion, you almost want to discourage a discussion.
turns.zh: 这太有意思了。具体来说，就是那些只需更新信息、不需要展开讨论的消息，我们甚至应该尽量避免引发讨论。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, I mean, it has the commenting, but it's not the same tool. And, by the way, Slack is amazing, we use it. It's just that for this thing, it wasn't working for us. And so, we wanted to move that somewhere else.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是说Slack确实有评论功能，但这毕竟不是同一款工具。顺便说一句，Slack确实很棒，我们也一直在用。但这次它对我们来说效果不佳。所以我们就想把这些功能转移到其他地方。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like, the more I dig into the Shopify way of working, the more fun stuff I never expected emerges. I'm curious what else is going to emerge. So we've been talking about ways that y'all, and you specifically, have created intensity, especially in the engineering organization. And then, you've also shared just broadly Shopify. What else is on that list? What else have you found helps create more kilojoules per hour?
turns.zh: 我感觉，越深入了解Shopify的办公方式，就越能发现许多意想不到的妙处。我很好奇接下来还会有什么新发现。我们一直在讨论你们，尤其是你，如何在工程团队中营造高效的工作氛围。还有，你也分享了Shopify整体的运营经验。接下来还有哪些措施？你还发现了哪些能提升团队效率的做法？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, so again, I think there's nothing, I would say again, start from the beginning, there's nothing more than pair programming, because literally you can't do anything else but be on your computer. So pair programming is the number one. I will say, the weekly cadence helps a lot, right, which you mentioned. Again, which is part of GSD, which is sharing the updates, and then the six-week reviews, that does a lot. On the other side, we also have a lot of metrics and alerts that help us see when potentially things might be happening in the system that can allow us to be like, "Hey, wait a sec, there's too many things going on of this type. We probably have to sit back and reset and figure out what's going on." (00:41:56): So one thing that happened, for example, was we started seeing that it was taking a lot of time to develop in our admin, like engineers at Shopify developing in the admin. So we called, what's called, a code yellow, which is before code red. But code yellow is this idea of like, "Hey, we're going to call a code yellow on the admin." We want to make sure that the developer experience inside Shopify is really good. It should be easy to start up the repo. It should be easy to make changes, it should be easy to see the changes. And so, those are the things that, again, we can create intensity, because this code yellow allows the champion to tap anyone on the shoulder and say, "Stop what you're doing and come help this thing." Which is an infrastructure layer thing. And by building out this infrastructure, it allows you to go fast. It takes longer to build infrastructure, but it makes you go fast forever afterwards, right? (00:42:41): I'll actually give you an example of one of these. So, we in 2020, 2021, the heyday of pandemic, obviously, there was a crypto summer again and crypto was going nuts. And we were sitting back and saying, "Wow, a lot of our merchants are now asking for NFT gating." NFT gating, which is, "If you have the token, you can now go into the storefront and see my products. You can see my prices and you can check it out, but only if you have the token." And, we were getting a lot of demand from merchants to be like, "We want to do this. We want to sell an NFT. And we want our buyers to have the NFT to have this great experience." And we're like, "We agree. We want you to be able to do whatever you want. And so, we want to build this for you too." (00:43:18): And, sitting with Toby, he's like, "You guys are thinking about it wrong." He goes, "How long would it take to build NFT gating?" I'm like, "I don't know. Two, three weeks." He goes, "Now, how long would it take to build a platform layer, which exposes APIs so anyone could build NFT gating in one hour?" I'm like, "I don't know. Two, three months." He goes, "Do that." He goes, "Because you don't know what they're going to build on top of the platform." NFT gating is one thing, one use case, but if you spend the time to build out the infrastructure layer, he calls it putting gas in the tank, if you put the gas in the tank, people could drive on that gas for a long time going forward. And so, he goes, "I always want you to think about..." And the key part was, "What can you build so anyone could build this in one hour?" Right? (00:44:00): So, he does this thing to us all the time where he goes, "Oh, this should only be..." He'll say it and people get the wrong thing. He'll say, "Oh, you could write this in a day." And what he means is, "What has to be true so that you could write this in a day? What infrastructure do you need?" And, he actually develops this way. He will write code against an API that doesn't exist, because he's like, "You know what should exist here? This API." He'll write the code, he'll go back and forth and refine the client on the server, and then he'll go, "This is correct, the correct client code. Now, let me go implement the server code." (00:44:31): And this is notion of building things as infrastructure that sound slower today, because it's going to take... It's two, three months, instead of two or three weeks. But after that, the things that people built on top, right, were so easy to build, there were so many more scenarios that were emerged. It's just a different way of thinking about software. And, it's intensity in a different way, it's intensity around building this infrastructure layer, which we want to build quickly, but takes two or three months, in this case, but then can get everyone building on top of our infra in a much, much quicker way. And of course, who knows what can flourish from there?
turns.zh:
是的，再说一次，我认为没有什么秘诀，我还是要从头说起。最重要的就是结对编程，因为你除了坐在电脑前别无他法。所以结对编程是头等大事。我要说，每周的汇报节奏非常有帮助，正如你提到的。这也是GSD的一部分——分享进展报告，以及每六周一次的评审，这些都起到了关键作用。另一方面，我们还有很多指标和警报机制，能帮助我们及时发现系统中可能出现的问题，比如“嘿，等等，系统里这种情况太多了，我们得停下来重整思路。”  

（00:41:56）举个例子，我们发现Shopify后台开发工程师花费大量时间开发。于是我们启动了代码黄色警报，这是代码红色警报之前的预警机制。代码黄色警报意味着“后台开发停下来，优先处理这个问题”。我们致力于确保Shopify的开发者体验良好，能轻松启动代码仓库、进行修改并查看更改。通过建立这样的基础设施，团队能快速推进工作。虽然搭建基础设施耗时，但之后就能保持高效。  

（00:42:41）我举个例子。2020、2021年疫情期间，市场对加密货币的热情高涨。我们收到大量商家需求，要求实现NFT门控功能，即“持有特定代币的用户才能访问店铺、查看商品和价格并完成购买”。我们迅速响应，认为这是一个绝佳的商业机会。托比却问：“开发NFT门控要多久？”我回答：“两三周。”他反问：“那开发一个支持NFT门控的平台层呢？只需一小时。”我说：不知道，可能两三个月。他说：“那就做吧。”因为他深知，用户可能基于这个平台层开发出更多应用。  

（00:43:18）他常用“加油”来激励团队：“把基础设施搭好，人们就能长期受益。”每次他都用反问激发思考：“要实现什么功能才能一小时完成？”
他的开发方式是这样的：他会针对一个尚不存在的API编写代码，因为他会想：“你知道这里应该有这个API吗？”他会先写代码，然后反复调整服务端和客户端的代码，最后再说：“这就是正确的客户端代码。现在让我去实现服务端代码吧。”（00:44:31）  
这种将事物构建为基础设施的理念在当下听起来可能更慢，因为它需要两到三个月的时间，而不是两到三周。但在这之后，人们在其之上构建的应用变得非常容易，涌现出了更多的场景。这只是一种不同的软件开发思维方式。这种思维方式的重点在于快速构建基础设施层，在这种情况下需要两到三个月的时间，但随后能让所有人以更快的速度在我们的基础设施之上进行开发。当然，谁知道从这里能涌现出什么样的创新呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's interesting and it makes sense that so much of the way you all think is about building the best possible platform, versus the, necessarily, best possible point solution for someone. And it also explains why you spend so much time in crafting really great code and pair programming, because again, it's a platform for other people to build stuff on. So, I think, a lot of this is very useful, especially for platform businesses.
turns.zh: 很有趣也很合理的是，你们大家思考问题的方式大多聚焦于搭建尽可能出色的平台，而不是为某人量身打造最佳的点解决方案。这也解释了为什么你们会花大量时间编写优质代码和进行结对编程——毕竟这是一个供他人开发的平台。所以我认为，这其中很多理念都非常实用，尤其对平台型企业而言。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: No, exactly. And actually, you're making me think of a stat. So, last year, maybe a tangent, but I tweeted out that GitHub Copilot has written over 1 million lines of code for Shopify. And people are like, "Oh my god." And it got picked up. And everyone's talking about it. And I go, "I don't know why is everybody getting so crazy, because what I want to see is GitHub Copilot deleting 1 million lines of code." That's when you know we're actually at this point where this is close to an engineer. Right? And so, we famously have deleted millions of lines of code this year, because we were trying to focus on, again, the sunk cost and rebuilding things elegantly, or you don't need this anymore and rebuilding. And I even tweeted out, I think someone said, "Oh, Shopify is in the top 10 Ruby code bases in the world." And I said, "I never want to see us on this list again." We shouldn't be gunning for number one, we should be gunning for number 100, right? We want to be not on this list. Right? Someone else can take the crown.
turns.zh: 没错，确实如此。说到这儿，我突然想起一个数据。去年，我在推特上提到GitHub Copilot为Shopify编写了超过100万行代码。人们都惊呼：“天哪！”这条消息被疯狂转发，引发热议。我当时回应道：“我不明白大家为何如此激动，因为我更希望看到GitHub Copilot删除100万行代码。” 这恰恰说明，我们正朝着工程师视角迈进，对吧？今年我们大规模删除了数百万行代码，专注于沉没成本和优雅重构——比如某些功能已不再需要，就果断舍弃。我甚至在推特上看到有人说：“Shopify跻身全球十大Ruby代码库之列。” 我回应道：“我再也不想看到我们上这份榜单了。” 我们不该争第一，而该争第一百名，对吧？让别人去争冠吧。
