turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, so there's a few things, right? One is, the more context you can fit in your head around a code base. And you can never really fit all of Shopify in your head, because it's a big complicated set of tools we give to merchants. But, the more you can simplify, the much easier everything becomes, resiliency, performance, reliability, maintainability, all the illities become much, much, much easier when the code base is simple. Now, all you need really is the mandate of like, "Oh, well, let's look at this code. And, if I could start this today, would I really build this thing? Or do I now have enough domain expertise to say, 'Oh no, this is the right solution?' So can I delete start over and build this more easily?" And now, everything else becomes easy to build on top of. (00:48:04): And so, routinely, we have a delete code club, we have hack days, which happens two or three times a year, where there's always one team that is focused on deleting code. They even have a manual, "Here's how to find things to delete." And, it's amazing. We almost always delete. I don't know if this is good or bad. We can always almost find a million plus lines of code delete, which is insane. But, at the same time, I applaud the teams for going after the cruft and the code base. And everything gets easier, right? Codelets loads faster. It's easier to understand. (00:48:34): This is why when I look at GitHub stats, you shouldn't really look at... I think Google put out and said, "Oh, 25% of all code is now written by AI." I'm like, "Where's the delete? Where is the 25% of all code is deleted by AI?" Right? This is where we have to start thinking about it. Because, the right code is never the volumous lines of code metric. It's always something else. It's always elegance. And that's where we have to think about. So, it is something that, as part of us being long-term infrastructure thinking, we really do care about that.
turns.zh: 是的，有几个关键点，对吧？首先，你需要尽可能多地在脑海中构想代码库的上下文。虽然你永远无法完全掌握Shopify的所有复杂功能，毕竟我们为商家提供的是一套庞大的工具集，但越是能简化代码，所有问题——弹性、性能、可靠性、可维护性——都会变得容易得多。当代码库简单化时，所有问题都变得容易许多。现在，你只需要一个指导方针，比如：“好吧，让我们看看这段代码。如果今天从头开始重写，我还会构建这个东西吗？或者现在我是否有足够的领域专业知识来判断‘不，这才是正确的解决方案’？所以我能否删除重写，让构建更轻松？” 然后，其他一切都变得易于构建。（00:48:04）：因此，我们定期举办“删除代码俱乐部”活动，平均每年举办两到三次，每次都有一个团队专注于删除代码。他们甚至有一份手册，指导如何查找可删除的代码片段。这真是令人惊叹。我们几乎总能删除数百万行代码，这太疯狂了。但与此同时，我为那些致力于清理代码库和优化代码的团队点赞。一切都变得更简单了，对吧？代码加载更快，也更容易理解。（00:48:34）：这就是为什么当我查看GitHub统计数据时，我觉得不应该只看……我记得谷歌曾声称“25%的代码现在由AI编写”。我当时就想，“那删除的代码呢？25%的代码被AI删除了吗？” 对吧？这正是我们需要开始思考的问题。因为，正确的代码从来都不是以代码行数为衡量标准的。它总是关乎优雅性。这才是我们需要关注的重点。因此，作为长期基础设施规划的一部分，我们确实非常重视这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love this, in part, because it connects to the topic we're talking about, which is speed, velocity, intensity, smaller code base, cleaner, better code base allows you to move faster. I used to be an engineer actually. But, both my engineering brain and my PM brain, I love the idea of killing stuff that's useless, fixing, making code cleaner, and better, and more durable. In reality, very hard for companies to prioritize this thing. Is there anything you found that helps you do that? You mentioned hack days and weeks are one part of that. Probably helps that Toby's an engineer and he understands the value of this stuff. But I guess, for folks that want to do this more, any advice?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个观点，一部分原因是它与我们正在讨论的主题相关——速度、效率、强度、更小的代码库、更简洁、更优质的代码库能让行动更迅速。实际上，我曾是一名工程师。但无论是作为工程师的思维，还是作为产品经理的思维，我都热衷于淘汰无用的部分，修复代码，提升代码的简洁性和可靠性。现实中，公司往往很难优先考虑这些问题。你有没有发现什么有用的方法？你提到黑客日和黑客周是其中一部分。这可能与托比（Toby）本身是工程师且深知这些价值有关。但我想，对于那些想更深入推进的人，有什么建议吗？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah. So actually, when we're building something, we think of it in one of three buckets. We're like, "Are you building an experiment, a feature, or infrastructure?" And, once you bucket things, you can say, "Oh, it's an experiment." You're like, "Cool. This is not infra. This is like, we're trying something to learn." And, by the way, that might turn into an experiment or infra, but it starts off as an experiment. Now, if you're building a feature, a feature is basically you're taking advantage of an existing piece of infra, right? So, token gating is the example I gave. If you could now build that in one hour, you would probably say, "Oh, we have the right infra below it." (00:50:14): But if you did what Toby does, which is, he's like, "Here's the infra I wish existed. Here's the feature. The feature might be quick to build, but now I have to go and build the infra." You're now slotting yourself into infra land, which is like, that could take longer, but you're now enabling it for a bunch of use cases. You don't have to think about it at once, because you may have people using your API in a different way. (00:50:32): So, I think you have to slot yourself. Now, how do people get into this mode? It is super, super hard. And, I would say, Toby is the secret sauce here, because he pushes us to think about things as infra almost all the time. I mean, one of the things that annoys me the most probably is that I'll always come to him and say, "Hey, we can do A or B." And he looks at me and he goes, "You know what I'm going to say, right?" I'm like, "You're going to say go back and generate more options." Because he doesn't like those. "I don't like A or B. Come back when you have something else." Right? Actually, maybe I'll tell you a little anecdote. He has a story where he says, "There are unlimited amount of wrong options for any problem. There's probably 10,000 right options, but everybody stops at the first right one, instead of what you should be spending all your time on, because the options that don't work, you're not going to spend time on. But you have to figure out which of the 10,000 options is the right one and spend time in what are all these right options? Don't just stop at the first one." (00:51:24): And so, when I come to and say, "A or B." I'm picking two of the 10,000. And he's like, "That's not what I... Go back and generate more options, because those are not the optimal ones." So, he is quite the philosopher on these things. And it does really change the way the company works, because he'll push you on these things. And then, we over time learn to spot the same patterns. And I learned to push my team on infra, and deleting code, and making things simple, because by the way, who doesn't want to get free stuff? Right? Free performance, free, easy to navigate code base, free maintainability, free resiliency,, because now, we went and did the hard work of deleting. It is hard. But that goes back to the beginning, right? Choose the hard thing. Don't just build the feature-
turns.zh: 是的。实际上，当我们开发某个东西时，我们会将其归入三个类别之一。我们会想：“你是在做实验、开发功能，还是搭建基础设施？”一旦对事物进行分类，你就能判断：“哦，这是一个实验。”你会说：“酷。这不是基础设施。这只是我们在尝试新东西以获取经验。”顺便说一句，它可能最终会演变成实验或基础设施，但最初它就是一个实验。现在，如果你正在开发一个功能，基本上，就是在利用现有的基础设施，对吧？比如我提到的令牌门控例子。如果你能在一小时内完成开发，你可能会说：“哦，我们已经有合适的基础设施了。” （00:50:14）但如果像托比那样做，他会说：“这是我希望存在的基础设施。这是功能。功能可能很快就能开发，但现在我必须去搭建基础设施。” 你现在就陷入了基础设施领域，这可能需要更长时间，但你为一系列用例提供了支持。你不必一次性考虑所有问题，因为可能有人会以不同的方式使用你的API。（00:50:32）所以，我认为你必须给自己定位。那么，人们如何进入这种模式呢？这非常非常困难。我想说，托比是其中的秘诀，因为他几乎总是促使我们把事情视为基础设施。我最烦恼的一件事就是，我总是去找他说：“嘿，我们可以做A或者B。”他看着我说：“你知道我要说什么的，对吧？” 我说：“你会让我回去生成更多选项。” 因为他不喜欢这些选项。“我不喜欢A或B。等你有其他想法再来吧。” 对吧？实际上，我可以讲个小故事。他有一个故事，他说：“对于任何问题，都存在无限个错误的选项。可能有10,000个正确的选项，但每个人都会在第一个正确选项上停下，却没有花时间去思考那些真正重要的选项，因为那些不起作用的选项，你根本不会去花时间。但你必须从10,000个选项中找出正确的那个，并花时间研究所有这些正确的选项？不要只停在第一个上。” （00:51:24）所以，当我去说：“A或B。” 我只是从10,000个选项中选了两个。而他说：“这不是我要的...回去生成更多选项，因为那些不是最优的。” 所以，他在这方面确实是个哲学家。这确实改变了公司的运作方式，因为他会不断督促你。在此过程中，我们逐渐学会识别相同的模式。我学会了在基础设施方面推动我的团队，删除代码，让事情变得简单，因为说真的，谁不想要免费的东西呢？对吧？免费的性能，免费的，易于导航的代码库，免费的可维护性，免费的弹性，因为现在，我们去做了删除代码的艰苦工作。确实很难。但这又回到了开头，对吧？选择困难的路。不要只开发功能——

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: The beginning, right? Choose the hard thing. Don't just build the feature, go make the feature easy to build.
turns.zh: 开头，对吧？选择困难的路。不要只开发功能，去让功能易于开发。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like there's just more and more good stuff. What else is there that might be helpful to folks while you're thinking about it? And interesting, I was reading your tweet where you shared a lot of this advice, and you mentioned this briefly, but I think it's important with pair programming, one of the benefits is there's no multitasking. You're not checking Twitter, Slack while you're working because you're there being watched. And I could see why that is more productive just innately.
turns.zh: 我觉得好东西真是越来越多了。在你思考的时候，有没有什么其他可能对大家有帮助的建议呢？有意思的是，我读到你分享这些建议的推文时，你简要提到了这一点，但我认为结对编程的一个好处就是没有多任务分心的问题。你不会一边在Slack上聊天，或者刷Twitter，一边工作，因为有人在监督你。所以我能理解为什么这样做效率更高，这很自然。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Oh no, for sure. Again, like underhand or free throws not only looks dumb, it feels dumb. People don't... They feel like they're wasting time sitting beside somebody and being like, "Well, I could be on my computer doing this thing." But together they are building a machine. Do you ever read the Undoing Project, which is about Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman, the famous philosopher.
turns.zh: 哦，确实。再说回来，比如在篮球比赛中，如果有人偷懒或者投篮不专心，既显得不专业，也让队友感到沮丧。人们不会……他们会觉得坐在旁边等别人做事是在浪费时间，还会想：“我本可以用电脑做其他事。”但当大家一起合作时，却能共同构建出一台机器。你读过《解构项目》这本书吗？讲的是阿莫斯·特维斯基和丹尼尔·卡尼曼，这两位著名的哲学家。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: By Michael Lewis, I think.
turns.zh: 作者是迈克尔·刘易斯吧。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Behavioral economist. Michael Lewis. Exactly. And he said the famous line was "Alone, we're okay, but together, we're a genius." Right? That's a pair programmer. That's like two people. You're like, "Ah, we're okay. But together, we're a genius." And that's exactly what pair programming is. And hopefully me plus an LLM is a genius as well, but that's the genesis of that thinking. So I would say another thing that helps us create intensity is demo culture. So as part of the GSD updates, hopefully we encourage people to share high fidelity updates, which is not just imagery, but actually a demo. One of the things that can go wrong with just their screenshots is you don't really get the full experience. You can't tell how slow things are or whatever, but with a demo, so you can put a link. We have this tool called Spin, which is an internal development environment like a cloud dev environment where you can say, "Hey, click here to try this on Spin, and then you can try it and you can see how it works." (00:53:52): Or they say, "Turn on a beta flag in your own store and then try it." And so this short circuits a lot of misunderstandings, because you're like "I'm going to try it." And you're not waiting until the end, especially with a beta flag. You're like, "Hey, it's in my store. I just realized that I went in and now this page takes 20 seconds to load. Is that what you expect?" You're like, "Oh, we didn't find this use case." You're going to learn that much more quickly. (00:54:13): And that creates, again, intensity on the fidelity of the feedback you're getting because famously, some of our PM team will create a friction log. They'll be like, "I am walking.." They'll just create a screen share, create a video and go, "I'm walking through. I turn on the beta flag, I'm walking through this experience. Here's my feedback on the experience." And you're getting this high fidelity throughput coming back to you that you're like, "Okay, let's fix these things for next week's iteration and then share another beta flag and say, 'Okay, try it now. Try it now. Try it now.'" And so you're not debating about status reports, you're kind of debating about the experience.
turns.zh: 行为经济学家。迈克尔·刘易斯。没错。他说过一句名言：“单独行动时，我们还不错，但团队协作时，我们就是天才。”对吧？这就是结对编程的精髓。希望我和LLM也能成为天才，但这就是这种思维方式的起源。所以我觉得另一个有助于提升专注度的因素是演示文化。作为GSD更新的部分，我们鼓励大家分享高保真更新内容，不只是图片，而是实际的演示。仅仅截图可能无法传达完整体验，比如加载速度慢之类的问题。但通过演示，你可以附上链接。我们有个叫Spin的工具，是内部开发环境，类似云端开发环境，你可以说：“嘿，点击这里在Spin上试试。”或者他们会说：“在你自己的店里启用测试标签然后试试。”这样能避免很多误解，因为你会说：“我要试试。”而不用等到最后阶段，特别是启用测试标签后，你会说：“哦，我发现加载页面要20秒。这是你们预期的吗？”你会说：“哦，我们没想到会出现这种情况。”这样你能更快地发现问题。（00:53:52）这又能提升反馈的真实性，因为我们PM团队有些人会创建摩擦日志。他们会说：“我正在操作……” 他们会截图、录制视频，然后说：“我正在演示整个过程。我启用了测试标签，体验如下。以下是我的反馈。” 这样你就能得到高保真反馈，接着改进，下周再分享新的测试标签，让大家继续试用。这就避免了讨论状态报告，转而专注于实际体验。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I'm trying to think broadly all the things you've shared, kind of how they fit together that allow you to move this fast. And I just looked up a few stats to give people a sense of just the size of the company today and how successful it has been as they hear the stuff we're talking about. So you guys are about 11,000 employees, something like that according to the Googles. And you're hitting not necessarily all-time highs on market cap because COVID gave you guys a big boost for a while, but you're kind of coming back to this insane valuation that you all had during COVID. So it's essentially all-time highs at a 10,000 plus person company moving really fast, shipping constantly. People love the product. And it feels like one key of what you're describing is essentially this operating rhythm that creates these check-ins that keep people moving and focused on the right sorts of tools and getting them quick feedback if they're moving in the wrong direction.
turns.zh: 接下来，我想全面思考一下你们分享的所有内容，以及这些内容如何协同运作，让你们能如此高效地推进业务。为了让大家更直观地感受公司现状和取得的成功，我刚查阅了一些数据。根据谷歌搜索结果，你们目前约有11,000名员工。尽管市值尚未创下历史新高（毕竟新冠疫情曾短暂推高过市值），但你们的估值已重回疫情期间的创纪录水平。在拥有1万多名员工的公司里，产品持续迭代、快速上线、用户反馈及时，这些成就堪称非凡。关键在于，你们形成了高效的运营节奏，通过定期沟通，引导团队专注于正确的开发方向，并能及时纠正偏离轨道的决策。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: And having the leaders pair with those people on those problems, not just checking in, but actually pairing with them on the problems that they're facing. So you get both the crafters who are working on the stuff and the leaders who may have broader context working together to kind of unblock.
turns.zh: 在解决问题时，领导者会与团队成员深度协作——不只是定期汇报，更是实时参与攻克难题。这种双向沟通机制，让开发者能专注于技术细节，领导者也能从更宏观的视角提供指导，共同突破难关。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's so interesting that it's like, again, people often are often like, "We don't need meetings. Get rid of all the meetings." You guys do that, but also, there's a lot of power in strategic meetings and check-ins. Another kind of bucket is just the engineering environment, engineers working with engineers, pair programming, things like that. There's a tool you mentioned for pair programming, Tuple, I think.
turns.zh: 有趣的是，虽然人们常说“没必要开会，把会议都取消了”，但你们恰恰做到了这一点。事实上，战略性会议和定期沟通往往能释放巨大能量。另一个关键点在于工程师生态——工程师之间深度协作，比如结对编程。你们提到的结对编程工具“Tuple”就值得关注。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Tuple. Yeah. It's funny because we use it exclusively, but we actually have this line internally, we call it, Shopify should be a crafters' paradise. It should be the place where crafters come to practice their craft and get better at their craft. Obviously, resonates from a lot of the engineering crafters, but it's not only engineering, it's UX and PM and ML, all the places where you'd want those people to actually have a great experience. We want them to come to Shopify because we believe this is the best place for that.
turns.zh: 元组。是的。说来有趣，我们日常使用它，但实际上我们内部有这样一句话：Shopify应该成为手工艺者的天堂。这里应该成为手工艺者们来施展技艺、不断精进的场所。显然，这句话引起了许多工程师手工艺者的共鸣，但这不只是针对工程师，还适用于用户体验、产品管理和机器学习等领域——所有你希望这些人才能获得卓越体验的领域。我们希望他们选择Shopify，因为我们坚信这里是实现这一目标的最佳之地。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. I just wrote a note down of just how you set up your teams for success. Oh, just avoid distractions. So I think the pair programming helps the workspace, workplace shift from Slack helps. I think you're also very firm on their working hours. You basically don't let...
turns.zh: 我太喜欢了。我刚刚写了一份笔记，记录了你们如何为团队的成功做好铺垫。哦，还有就是避免干扰因素。比如，结对编程有助于优化工作环境；将工作场所从Slack转移到其他平台也很有效。我觉得你们在工作时间管理上也非常严格。基本上不允许员工...

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不允许。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No. Okay. [inaudible 00:57:04]
turns.zh: 不允许。好的。[00:57:04不可听清]

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: No, not really. Yeah. We're not super firm on working hours from that perspective, but we do have a lot of people on East Coast time zones. A lot of stuff happens then, but we do have people all over the world. But I did mention we do have the check-ins and the six-week reviews on the cadence. So that six week cycle does give you a little bit of the, what did you get done and are you blocked mentality. And you can expect coming in a couple of times and being like, "Hey, we didn't get a lot done being unblocked." For you to change your approach to go, "Okay, I don't want to go to another review where we didn't get a lot done." So what am I doing this time to make sure we unlock a lot of progress? And that check-in can give you that ammo to be like, "Let's do this this time."
turns.zh: 嗯，不完全是。从这个角度来看，我们对工作时间的要求确实不算严格，但我们确实有很多员工在东部时区工作。很多工作都在那个时段开展，不过我们确实有分布在世界各地的员工。不过我之前提到过，我们确实有固定的每六周一次的汇报和回顾机制。这种六周一次的周期确实能让你清楚了解自己完成了哪些工作，哪些方面遇到了阻碍。这样你就能预期到，偶尔参加汇报时，会听到有人说：“嘿，我们这周没做多少事，还是有阻碍。”这时候你就会调整思路，改进方法，避免下次汇报时再出现类似情况。“这次我要怎么做才能取得更多进展呢？”这种汇报机制能给你提供动力，让你积极行动。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And you're also remote first as a company.
turns.zh: 对，你们公司一直推行远程办公。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Which I think is especially cool. Now a lot of companies are going back to not remote. You guys are staying remote. Why do you guys decide to do that? What have you seen as a big benefit of that?
turns.zh: 我觉得这点特别棒。现在很多公司都开始回归到非远程办公模式。但你们公司始终坚持远程办公。为什么会做出这样的决定？你们从中获得了哪些显著的益处？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, so we have this remote, so I like to call it 90% remote or 95% remote because we have these intentional IRL experiences. So every summer, we just started last year. Sorry, this year. We're doing this thing called Shopify Summit where we bring the whole company together, get together and it's a combination of talks plus hack days and it's a come together experience like food and parties and bands. And it's a super fun way to re-energize and rebuild your trust battery over time. And then we have this thing called bursts, which is, "Hey, you want to work on a problem? You need to prototype, you need to hack." People can just say, "Hey, I'm starting a burst. We're going to have five people. We're all going to go to Ottawa or Toronto or Montreal or somewhere else and we're going to talk about this problem and get together." (00:58:38): And so a combination of those two things mean throughout the year, you can recharge. We have the trust battery notion, which is how much trust can you have between people and it can deplete over time if you're remote. So then we have offices which are like, come in if you want. Like I mentioned, I come in once a week and now Toby moved to Toronto, so now I'm in three days a week. But it's like if you want to come in, you don't have to, right? Today, I work from home, but tomorrow, I'm going in. And that allows you, again, to have those random interactions and allow you to feel like, yeah, we're 90 plus percent remote. But I would say the main reason is we want to hire the best people in the world and those people can be anywhere and just happens to be that not all of them are near an office. (00:59:20): But again, with the bursting, here's a good example. For Black Friday, Cyber Monday, I encouraged all engineering leadership to come to Toronto. We're all going to be in the office watching the graphs. And then for hack days, I try to get people to go to the ports, which we have four of them, Toronto, Montreal, Ottawa, and New York, which again are come in if you want, but then get that IRL. And so it's kind of a little bit of a combo. I wouldn't call it hybrid though because you don't really have every Friday you come in or don't come in. It's more like, come in if you want.
turns.zh:
是的，我们确实是远程优先模式。我喜欢把我们称为90%远程或95%远程，因为我们有一些刻意安排的面对面交流机会。比如每年夏天，我们从去年开始举办Shopify峰会，把全公司员工聚集在一起。这是一个集讲座、黑客马拉松和社交活动于一体的盛会，有美食、派对和乐队表演。这种方式能有效激发活力，持续增强团队凝聚力。
然后还有“爆发式项目”（bursts）活动。“嘿，你想解决某个问题吗？需要做原型设计、黑客马拉松？”大家可以发起公告：“我们要开展一个爆发式项目，五个人参加，地点在渥太华、多伦多、蒙特利尔或其他城市，共同探讨这个问题。”（00:58:38）这两种方式相结合，让员工全年都能保持充电状态。我们引入了“信任电池”概念，衡量团队成员之间的信任程度。远程办公确实会消耗信任储备，所以我们设有办公室，员工可以根据需求到场。比如我每周去一次办公室，托比搬到多伦多后，现在我每周去三天。总之，只要你想来，随时可以到场。这能促进随机交流，让大家感受到，尽管90%以上员工远程办公，但我们始终保持着紧密的联系。
（00:59:20）但最重要的原因是，我们想招聘全球最优秀的人才，而这些人才可能分布在世界各地。并非所有人才都在办公室附近办公。（00:59:40）但回到爆发式项目，比如“黑色星期五”、“网络星期一”，我们鼓励所有工程团队领导到多伦多办公室观看数据图表。黑客马拉松活动时，我们也会组织员工前往四个办事处——多伦多、蒙特利尔、渥太华和纽约。同样，员工可以根据意愿选择到场，但这种面对面的交流确实能提升团队凝聚力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's so many things to talk about. This trust battery metaphor by the way is awesome. I've learned to use it also. And again, it's just basically everyone, your trust with someone is like, think of it as a battery that can deplete and grow and you should try to charge it up when you can and then use that charge over time.
turns.zh: 太多想聊的了。顺便说一句，这个信任电池比喻太棒了。我也学会了用它。再说一次，基本上每个人都适用——你和某人的信任关系就像一个电池，可能充放电。只要有机会就应该尽力充值，然后逐步消耗。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: And it can be strategic by the way. I've seen people use it as a... I'm pretty sure Toby says he starts everyone at 50% and then he gets to know you. And then I've seen people use it as the opposite, saying, "Hey, look, this team is hard charging. I'm going to start you at a hundred. Assume that you already have high trust, do the things, and only if you are doing things that are off alignment, does your trust battery deplete." So I've seen people use it, the terminology as a shortcut way to figure out how to work with somebody.
turns.zh: 这里面还有策略层面的运用。比如我见过有人用这个比喻："我会把每个人设定在50%的信任度，然后逐渐了解你。"还有人反其道而行之："嘿，看看这个团队充满活力，我一开始就设定100%的信任度，就当你已经高度信任对方了。只要你不做偏离正轨的事，信任度就不会下降。"所以我觉得人们用这个比喻，是把它当作快速建立合作关系的捷径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love just how first principles you all are, and there are so many things are so unique to how you operate and clearly it's working. And so I feel like we just keep going on and on. I want to talk about hiring. I know you have some pretty unique perspectives on how to hire people that are awesome, but also, hire them quickly. But before we get there, is there anything else that you think might be really valuable to share in terms of intensity, velocity, moving fast?
turns.zh: 我特别欣赏你们坚持第一性原理的态度。你们的运作方式有很多独特之处，而且显然很有效。所以我觉得我们可以继续深入探讨。我想谈谈招聘问题。你们在招聘人才方面有一些非常独特的见解，既要迅速招到合适的人，又要确保质量。但在深入之前，你们觉得在高强度、快速行动、快速迭代方面，还有什么值得分享的经验吗？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: I think the personality of the leadership team is quite intense. We have a lot of founders on the exec team, which are impatient, intense people by design. But even some of the non-founders are just accomplished people who tend to be pretty, we all have this attitude of impatience, and so maybe, I don't even know if that's a learned skill you can learn or if it just comes along with your personality, like genetics. But we typically, even at the leadership team, for example, we try to do, here's my weekly thread of all the things that are going on so that we can not only share, but also show progress on things. And then someone can jump in and say, "Oh, this thing you're doing, it relates to my thing that I'm doing over here." It creates this notion of, there's a lot going on all the time and we want to keep the vibes, keep the energy high. So a lot of high energy intense people.
turns.zh: 领导团队的个性非常强势。我们高管团队里有很多创始人，他们天生就是 impatient、intense 的人。即使不是创始人的，也都是非常有成就的人，他们也普遍有这种 impatience 的态度。可能这既是天生的，也和基因有关。但在领导团队里，我们会每周分享所有进展，这样不仅能分享信息，还能展示进展。然后有人会参与进来，说：“哦，你做的这个项目和我的工作方向很契合。” 这营造了一种随时有大量事情在进行的氛围，我们希望保持这种活力和热情。所以这里有很多充满活力的人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It reminds me while I was at Airbnb, it felt like no matter how well things are going, it always felt like Brian especially is just pedal to the metal. No matter how well things are going, it's not going well enough. How do we go faster? How do we do more?
turns.zh: 这让我想起我在Airbnb的经历。无论事情进展得多顺利，布莱恩（Brian）总是全力以赴。即使一切进展顺利，也总觉得还不够快。我们要如何再快一点？如何做得更多？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Well, I would actually go further. I think if you don't have two or three big projects that are on fire, you're probably not pushing hard enough because you're not really trying things that are outside of your... If everything's going well, are you really taking the risks you need to be taking? So I think you have to over-rotate a bit and there should be a few things on fire at all times, not because you should create that, but it should just happen because you're stretching into new things that potentially or you're going faster than you should have, or there's a new leader you've counted on early because all these things that should create this thing of it might work. And so you want to have a little bit of chaos at the edge.
turns.zh: 事实上，我甚至会更进一步。我认为如果你没有两三个正在推进的大项目，那说明你推动得还不够狠，因为你没有真正尝试突破自己的舒适区。如果一切都进展顺利，是不是意味着你没有承担足够的风险？所以你必须稍微加点压力，随时有几个项目在推进，不是因为你刻意去创造这些项目，而是因为你在尝试新事物、超越既定节奏，或者因为你过早地信任了某位新领导者——所有这些因素都可能创造出成功的条件。所以你需要在边缘保持一点混乱。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. And it may sound stressful and why would I want that? Why would I want to work with chaos and fires everywhere? But in reality, if you don't, your business is unlikely to become incredibly successful and that is even more stressful and painful.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样。虽然听起来压力很大，但为什么我要这样做呢？为什么要在混乱和危机四伏的环境中工作？但现实是，如果你不这样做，你的业务不太可能取得巨大成功，而这反倒会带来更大的压力和痛苦。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Correct. Yeah, it's like the opposite, right? It's like this idea of people feel like the comfort gives you stability, and really the uncomfort gives you stability because now you're constantly learning and that makes you more robust against things that could come across.
turns.zh: 没错。这简直是反其道而行之，对吧？人们总觉得舒适能带来稳定，但实际上不适感才能带来稳定，因为这样你才能不断学习，从而更从容地应对各种挑战。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Choosing the harder path, some might say. Okay, let's talk about hiring. You have some really interesting takes on hiring. One that I've heard about is that you don't like the interview process. You kind of like to prefer not to interview and do something instead. Talk about that.
turns.zh: 有些人可能会说，这就是选择更艰难的道路。好吧，那我们来谈谈招聘。你对招聘有一些很有趣的见解。我听说你不喜欢面试流程，你宁愿不面试而采取其他方式。能谈谈这个吗？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah. So throughout my career, what I've noticed is that, and I'm sure everybody, this is a dirty little secret, right? Interviews are not a good predictor of performance. We know this. We know this from studies. We know this. Everybody at their company knows this, where somebody interviewed well, wasn't as good in the job or the opposite, didn't interview well and then came in and was phenomenal. One example I have from my startup right before we came to Shopify was I hired two people for machine learning. One was a PhD, taught at the university, was like, oh my god, no brainer, was also recommended by an employee. We're like, "Oh my god, this person's going to be great." The other person was a dude I met at the coffee shop who had never had a software job but was just so interested in machine learning and person A, we let go within a few weeks because not a fit for our culture. (01:04:12): And person B was at our startup and is still at Shopify today and is a phenomenal machine learning engineer who literally at our Christmas party was like, "This is my first software job." We're like, "How?" It was just so cute. And we gave them both the shot. The key was I didn't use the resume in either way to bias. We brought them both in. We said, "Here's the environment." It was all pair programming at my startup. And so they pair program, and actually as an aside, I really believe in pair programming when I made people work in pair programming with my own money. I paid for two people to be on one computer. So that's how you know...
turns.zh: 是的。在我的职业生涯中，我发现（相信大家也都心知肚明）面试并不能很好地预测一个人的工作表现。我们都知道这一点——这从研究中就能看出来。每个公司的人都知道，面试表现出色的人在实际工作中表现不佳，或者相反，面试表现不佳的人后来却表现出色。举个例子，在我创办Shopify之前的初创公司，我招聘了两个机器学习工程师。一个是博士学位，曾在大学任教，大家都觉得“天啊，这简直是必然之选”，甚至还有员工推荐。我们当时想：“这人肯定很棒。”另一个是我在咖啡店遇到的人，从未有过软件工作经验，但对机器学习充满热情。结果A被我们辞退了，因为不符合我们的文化。（01:04:12）而B至今仍在Shopify，是一位杰出的机器学习工程师。在我们的圣诞派对上，他说：“这是我第一份软件工作。”我们惊讶道：“怎么可能？”真是太可爱了。关键是我们没有用简历来带偏。我们让两人都进来，告诉他们：“这就是我们的工作环境。”当时我的初创公司全部采用结对编程。结果两人都进行了结对编程。顺便说一句，我非常推崇结对编程——我曾用自己的钱让员工结对编程，让两人共用一台电脑。可见……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Less than half the code.
turns.zh: 写出的代码不到一半。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. Right. Less than half the code. But anyway, so pairing. And it was pretty clear after just a few weeks, I would say let's say up to three months is the amount of time I give people, that person A wasn't going to work out than person B was. So what I really like to do is use this race car analogy. If I told you, "Hey, I want to go hire the best race car driver," there's not really that many questions you could ask them except for put them in the car. And so the same thing happens with us is that of course, we have to do interviews, but we do really spend time in the 30, 60, 90 days to make sure that the thing that they are bringing actually lines up with what we need at Shopify. And you should also be transparent with people because if it's not a fit, it's actually good for them and you to figure that out as quickly as possible because they could be amazing somewhere else. (01:05:39): We mentioned the chaotic environment and fast moving environment Shopify is, that's not for everyone, but that's okay, right? We're not looking for... We've talked about that we want to be as the best 10,000 person company in the world. We're not looking for millions of people. We just need the best 10,000. And so if it's not a fit, it's in your interest and our interest to figure that out quickly so that you can go somewhere where you will be amazing and for us to have the people who will be amazing at Shopify. And so job trials, I'm a huge fan of, which leads me to intern programs, what a great interview process because you now have real work product from somebody for four months. They get to see what it's like to be at Shopify for four months. We get to see what it's like for them to be at Shopify for four months, and that can turn into a full-time gig. (01:06:21): And that's a great interview process because you literally know exactly. You don't have to... I'll give you a funny example. I think I've heard a company where, "Oh, we have an intern process and then afterwards, we interview them for full-time." I'm like, "What are you going to learn from let's say even eight hours of interviews that you're not going to have learned from four months of real work experience?" And so there's just things like that. You just got to look at the work product. And so I'm a big fan of job trials, and in my previous companies, like you mentioned, I almost didn't interview anybody. I almost just said, "Come in and work." And it allowed us... We had a much higher in the first 90 days, like 20% attrition before 90 days because it just didn't work out. But those after 90 days, we had less than 1% attrition because they knew exactly what they're getting into and we knew exactly how they were going to fit.
turns.zh:
是的，没错。没错。代码量不到一半。不过说回配对机制。几周之后就很明显了，比如说我给新人最多三个月的观察期，我就能判断出A和B谁更适合我们。所以我特别喜欢用赛车手的比喻。如果我跟你说：“嘿，我想去雇佣最顶尖的赛车手。”除了让他们上车试试，基本没别的可问的。我们招聘新人也是这样，虽然必须进行面试，但在入职后的30天、60天、90天里，我们会花大量时间确保他们带来的技能与Shopify的需求完美契合。另外，我们也要对候选人保持透明——如果不合适，尽快告知他们才是负责任的做法，因为他们在别处可能会大放异彩。  

（01:05:39）：我们提到Shopify是一个混乱且快节奏的环境，这并不适合所有人，但这没关系，对吧？我们的目标是成为全球最出色的万人公司，不追求数量，而是专注于质量。所以如果不合适，无论是对你还是对我们来说，尽快确认都符合双方利益，这样你就能去其他地方大展身手，而我们也能找到能在Shopify大放异彩的人才。  

（01:06:21）：我特别推崇工作试用期，这也让我想到了实习项目。这是一个绝佳的面试流程，因为你能在四个月内得到真实的工作成果。他们能亲身感受在Shopify工作的四个月，我们也能评估他们的表现，最终可能转为全职。  

（01:06:21）：这是一个高效的面试机制，因为你能精准评估能力。我听过有些公司先进行实习，再面试转正。我就想说：“八小时的面试能比四个月的实际工作经验获取更多信息吗？”所以关键在于看工作成果。  

（01:06:21）：在之前的公司，我几乎不进行正式面试，直接让他们上岗。这样90天内的离职率高达20%，因为不合适的人很快被淘汰。但90天后离职率不到1%，因为双方都清楚彼此的诉求。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So in terms of the hiring process, you're still at Shopify. You're interviewing people, they're doing technical evaluations, things like that. But it sounds like there's a very strong setting of expectations. "We will hire you, but we'll actually clarify if this is a good fit in the first 30, 60, 90 days and we're going to do... We may let you go and there's a good chance we may let you go." Is that just the way you set things up?
turns.zh: 那么招聘流程方面，你现在还在Shopify。你会进行面试、技术评估之类的。但听起来你们设定了很高的期望值。“我们会雇佣你，但会在前30天、60天、90天里确认是否合适，之后可能会让你离开。”是这样设定的吗？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, I think the way to think about, it's more like we want to make the interview process as close to the real job as possible because by doing that, we can likely assess the skills that you have in your interview closer to what's happening in the job. So that's one. Two, we have this interview step called the life story where we try to figure out if, are all the experiences you've had up until now actually going to be... Does it show that you are a curious person with range? Because if it does, that's likely more of someone who's going to be a fit. I had this famous line from somebody who said, "You know what I don't like about resumes?" I'm like, "What?" They go, "It tells you what you did, but it doesn't tell you why you did those things." (01:08:10): And it's such an interesting insight. Your resume should be a why, like why did you go from this company to this? That's the interesting part. Not that you are a PM at Microsoft and a PM at Stripe. It's like, why did you switch from Stripe to Microsoft? There's something interesting there. And so the life story is trying to pull that out. It's like, why did you make the decisions? What did you do in your past that was interesting? Are you curious? I always thought... I read this great book, Range by David Epstein. That book was maybe one of the hardest books for me to read in my life because every page I was like, "I don't believe it." I kept thinking I was a specialist. I kept turning the page going, "I don't like this data that keeps showing that generalists are better." And then by the end, I realized that I'm a generalist. It took me so long to realize, and funny for me because I ended up redesigning the compensation system for Shopify, even though I'm an engineer. (01:08:56): So I still thought of myself as an engineer through and through, even though I work on recruiting and HR and all these other things. But I think that that's what we're trying to tease. And then yes, in that first period, we actually have a survey that goes over Slack that says, "Hey, how happy are you with the person that you hired?" And that should, in conversation with the person, you should give them the feedback to figure out, "Hey, are there things you need to adjust to better fit in and make sure the expectations are set up?" But then also, together with the person, figure out, "Hey, if you're not feeling this, let's find you either a different role in the company or somewhere else because we want the people here to have high impact." But that person should have high impact somewhere, could be at Shopify, could be in the same role, could be in a different role, could be at a different company. But that's a good thing for everybody.
turns.zh:
是的，我认为面试流程的设计理念是尽可能贴近真实的工作场景，这样才能更准确地评估应聘者的能力与岗位要求的契合度。首先，我们引入了一个名为"人生故事"的环节，通过深入挖掘申请者过往经历，判断他们是否具备好奇心、探索欲和跨领域的适应能力。这类特质正是我们寻找的理想人才特质。

我曾听过这样一句名言："简历只告诉你做了什么，却不解释为什么这么做。"（01:08:10）这句话深刻揭示了简历的局限性。简历本应传达出申请者的决策逻辑与成长历程，比如从一家公司跳槽到另一家背后的动机。这种深度探讨才能真正展现出应聘者的潜力与匹配度。

《多面手》一书让我深有共鸣。书中提到，通才型人才比专才更具竞争力，这一观点曾让我深感震惊。尽管书中数据令人信服，但我始终难以接受这个结论，坚信自己是工程师中的"专家"。直到参与Shopify薪酬体系重构时，我才意识到自己其实是通才型人才。这种转变用了很久，但过程充满趣味。

回到面试流程，我们会通过Slack调查收集反馈，了解应聘者对新同事的满意度，并及时提供反馈建议。同时，我们会与候选人共同探讨职业发展路径，确保双方期望清晰。如果发现不适应现有环境，我们会帮助他们调整方向，或推荐其他职位或公司。这最终是为了确保每位员工都能在Shopify发挥最大价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And then do you actually do work trials with new engineering hires, or is that something you aspire to do?
turns.zh: 那你们是否真的会对新入职的工程师进行工作试用，还是说这只是你们的愿景？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, I would love to do it. It's hard to do with the volume resumes we get, but we do do it at scale with the internship program. So like 2025, we're going to hire a thousand interns, and that is going to give me a thousand job trials to pick the top X percent of those to come to Shopify full time.
turns.zh: 是的，我非常希望能这样做。但面对海量简历，这确实是个挑战。不过我们通过实习项目已经在大规模实践了。比如2025年，我们计划招收1000名实习生，这将为我们提供1000次工作试用机会，最终选拔出最优秀的X%加入Shopify全职团队。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So just to double-click on that, so you're hiring a thousand interns over the course of the year. That's a lot. And the idea there is these folks are actually useful building useful things, and it's an interview process for the internship.
turns.zh: 再详细说一下，就是你们全年会招收1000名实习生。这数量可真不少。实习项目本质上也是一种面试过程，对吧？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, I think it's two things. One is some people look at an internship program as community service. Let's give back to the community. Let's hire early talent. And I'm like, "Hold on a sec. Are you telling me I could hire a thousand people over the year?" And they will come to work with an LLM and a brain because they're growing up in the age of AI. They will be useful to us because they come from a different generation and they have, in our case in commerce, they have a different experience about shopping and AI and bots and chat and voice and all these things. They'll be useful to us. We'll teach them some stuff as well. And then together we can decide if they might end up going somewhere else, in which case, we have the Shopify imprint on them going to whatever other company, which is I think a positive, or they might stay at Shopify and be useful over a longer period. (01:11:02): It seems like win, win, win. The other thing that was cool is after I did that tweet, a bunch of other CTOs messaged me and said, "Hey, we're going to hire 1,001 interns to beat you guys." And I'm like, "Great." Just from that one tweet, if I can get the early talent ecosystem restarted here after a really tough last few years and layoffs, it's great for everybody because now they're realizing that they also realize that these people are super valuable and they bring together a completely different set of skills. And by the way, here's a secret in pair programming, interns will always be more intense than the full-time. And so that also helps the flywheel of intensity go for it.
turns.zh: 是啊，我觉得这有两个原因。首先，有些人把实习项目视为社区服务项目。他们想回馈社会，招募早期人才。我就想：“等等，你是说我一年能招一千人吗？”这些实习生会带着法学硕士学位和敏锐的商业头脑加入公司，毕竟他们成长于人工智能时代。他们能为我们带来价值，因为他们来自不同时代，在商业领域，他们对购物、人工智能、聊天机器人、语音交互等领域有着独特的见解。我们也会教他们一些东西。然后我们可以一起决定他们是否会去其他公司——如果这样的话，他们身上带有Shopify的印记，无论去哪家公司，对我们来说都是积极的。或者他们可能会留在Shopify，长期为我们创造价值。（01:11:02）：这看起来是三赢局面。另一件很酷的事是，我发了那条推文后，很多CTO给我发消息说：“嘿，我们要招10001名实习生来超过你们。”我回复：“太好了。” 就凭那条推文，如果能在经历了过去几年的裁员风暴后，重启这里的早期人才生态，对大家都有好处，因为现在他们意识到这些年轻人非常有价值，能带来全新的技能组合。顺便说一句，关于结对编程有个秘密，实习生总是比全职员工更有冲劲。这也有助于形成良性循环。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It all just keeps coming back. Did the internship program emerge out of this co-op system that Canadian schools have and a Waterloo has a big co-op program?
turns.zh: 这话题总是一再回归。实习项目是从加拿大学校的合作教育体系演变而来的吗？滑铁卢大学的合作教育项目规模很大。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, I went to Waterloo. And so yeah, hint, hint. So I went to Waterloo and I did co-op and I did intern programs there. It was amazing. What a great experience, because what ends up happening is you leave Waterloo with your degree, but also with two years of experience because I did six four-month work terms, 24 months, and you end up walking. I think one of the big parts of it is just interview skills because I interviewed for 10 plus jobs every four months, and I did that six times. And so you come out having done lots... You have a lot of interview experience, but you also have work experience. And so just taking that to the next level, Shopify has always had interns. And what I felt like we needed to do was, again, restart this notion of early talent in the ecosystem. I would say one or two big differences with our intern program. (01:12:36): One is we're making them come in three days a week versus full remote. And the reason for that is, and we're doing it just in three offices right now in Montreal, Toronto and Ottawa. And the reason for that is because we want them to have a cohort because early talent is different than you and I who've been in the industry. We worked in office, we worked out of office. We're more comfortable with navigating partnership discussions and talking to people in different companies. But these people have not. They may have never worked anywhere. (01:13:02): And so to not have the IRL component would do them a disservice. And so we specifically made it in those ports and the people are traveling by the way, they're moving to Montreal to do the internship. It's great. And then if you're a mentor or manager for one of the interns, you have to at least see them like IRL once a month. So we're kind of making these experiences. And of course, they'll have a cohort of dozens of people that will be with them along the way. And so we think that'll just make their experience better. And of course, nothing like tapping someone on the shoulder and be like, "Have you seen this era before?" And so it's easier in an early talent situation. And then of course over time, if they become full-time, they can still come to the office. It's come if you want, but they can also go full remote.
turns.zh: 是的，我去过滑铁卢大学。所以，嗯，给你点提示。就是说，我去了滑铁卢大学，参加了那里的合作教育项目和实习项目。体验太棒了。那真是一段很棒的经历，因为最终你毕业时不仅拿到了学位，还获得了两年的工作经验——因为我做了六个为期四个月的工作实习，共24个月，最终毕业时你已经积累了丰富的实践经验。我认为其中很重要的一点是面试技巧，因为每四个月我要面试十多个职位，这样的经历重复了六次。所以毕业时你不仅拥有大量面试经验，还积累了实际工作经验。再进一步说，Shopify一直都有实习项目。我们觉得需要重新激发生态系统中早期人才的潜力。在我们的实习项目中，主要有两个方面的不同之处：（01:12:36）：一是我们要求他们每周到办公室三天，而不是完全远程办公。之所以这样做，是因为我们目前只在蒙特利尔、多伦多和渥太华的三个办公室开展这个项目。这样做的原因是，我们希望他们能形成一个学习小组，因为早期人才与我们这些在行业内工作过的人不同。我们曾在办公室工作，现在也在远程办公。我们更擅长处理合作伙伴关系讨论，跟不同公司的同事交流。但这些年轻人没有这些经验。他们可能从未在任何地方工作过。（01:13:02）所以没有线下的交流环节会对他们不利。因此我们特别安排了这些见面环节。顺便说一下，参与实习的人会到蒙特利尔参加项目。这很棒。然后，如果你是实习生的导师或经理，你至少每月要亲自与他们见面一次。所以我们在精心设计这些体验。当然，没有什么比得上拍拍某人肩膀说"你以前见过这个时代吗？"的场景了。在培养早期人才的环境中，这样做更容易。当然，随着时间推移，如果他们转为全职员工，他们仍然可以来办公室上班。可以随意来，也可以完全远程办公。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That is amazing. For folks that don't know anything about these co-op programs briefly, it's just basically while you're in school, before you graduated, during the summer, you go work at a company.
turns.zh: 太棒了。对于不了解这些合作教育项目的人简单说一下，在你上学期间，在毕业前，在夏天，你去一家公司工作。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, during the year. Okay.
turns.zh: 哦，是在学年期间。好的。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, it's during the year. So what happens at Waterloo is, what I did was I did eight months of school at the beginning. So two terms. My first co-op term was summer, but then it was work, school, work, school, alternating for the whole rest of my time at Waterloo.
turns.zh: 是的，是在学年期间。在滑铁卢大学，我先上了八个月的课，两个学期。我的第一个合作教育学期是在夏天，但之后就是工作、学习、工作、学习，整个在滑铁卢大学的剩余时间都是这样交替进行的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's like semesters alternating.
turns.zh: 就像学期交替一样。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Exactly. So every four months I did either school term or work time. So I was doing work in January sometimes and September sometimes. And it was super good because again, it also allowed me to be super intense at school for four months and then go to super intense work experience for four months. But yeah, it's a model that... I was just at Waterloo this week doing a talk, so I love that symbiotic relationship between Waterloo and the employers, by the way, not just Waterloo. Lots of schools do a summer program, UFT and others, lots of schools in the states.
turns.zh: 没错。所以每四个月我要么专注学业，要么投入工作。比如有时一月份在工作，有时九月份又开始学习。这真的很棒，因为这样既能让我在四个月里全身心投入学业，又能在接下来的四个月里全力投入工作。顺便说一句，我本周刚在滑铁卢大学做了一场演讲，我很欣赏滑铁卢大学与雇主之间这种互惠互利的关系——不只是滑铁卢大学，美国很多学校也开展暑期项目，比如UFT等。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Fun fact. So total tangent, I had a startup called Local Mine, started it in Montreal of all places. I'm not Canadian, but moved there for various reasons. It was awesome. And our first hire was actually from the co-op program. I don't know if it was Waterloo, his name is Nick Adams. And he applied. Just he saw our job posting, I think, and were like, "What is a co-op?" And he came to work and then he went back to school, and then we hired him, and then he ended up at Airbnb when we got a card.
turns.zh: 趣闻分享。说点题外话，我曾在蒙特利尔创办过一家名为Local Mine的初创公司。虽然我不是加拿大人，但出于各种原因搬到了那里。创业经历很棒。我们首位员工来自合作教育项目。我不确定他是否来自滑铁卢大学，但我记得他叫尼克·亚当斯。他看到我们的招聘信息后，问“什么是合作教育项目？”然后加入团队，完成学业后又回学校深造，后来我们把他转正，最后他去了Airbnb。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: There you go. So for us, actually, when I did my startup Helpful, I had one or two engineers, and then I actually literally just hired four interns because you hired them in February for May. And because I was doing pair programming, I had to make sure I had four full times by then. So I hired the interns in anticipation of having the full times. And I literally had, I think I was off by one week, so one intern had no pair for a week, but then after that in May, I had four full times, four interns, and then they paired the whole time.
turns.zh: 就是这样。实际上，当我创办Helpful公司时，最初有1-2名工程师，后来我直接雇了4名实习生，因为实习生是二月份招聘，五月份入职。由于我采用了结对编程模式，必须确保那时有四名全职员工。所以我提前雇了实习生，以便到五月份能有四名全职员工和四名实习生配合工作。唯一遗憾的是，有一位实习生那周没有结对搭档，但之后五月份所有人都顺利完成了结对编程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a journey. I want to talk about just one other topic real quick and then we'll wrap this up. And it's around XtremeLabs. So there's a bunch of stuff here. It feels like it's just like this tech mafia of Canada that a lot of incredible people emerged out of, and there's a whole bunch of stuff we can talk about. One fact I heard while you were there is you had a hundred reports, direct reports that reported to you.
turns.zh: 真是一段精彩的历程。我想再快速聊聊XtremeLabs。这里有很多故事。感觉加拿大科技界就像个“黑手党”般的圈子，涌现了许多杰出人才。我们可以聊很多话题。比如我在那里了解到，你有100名直接汇报给你的下属。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: 120 direct reports feels like a complete nightmare to me. Tell me why you decided to do that, if you'd recommend that for other people.
turns.zh: 对我来说，120名直接汇报的下属简直是个噩梦。能否谈谈你为何选择这样做？是否建议其他人也这样做？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, so what ended up happening there was we started off small. It was 10 people. When I got to XtremeLabs, I wasn't the founder, but I was very early on and I just had everyone report to me. And then as we grew, I just kept having those people report to me and I was trying to figure out, we talked about crafters and crafters paradise, this idea of people don't really... Their managers are useful, but I was trying to figure out could I solve the problems that they needed their manager for in other ways? So for example, what should I be working on? I was like, "Okay, well, we have product backlogs" or "I'm blocked on something," or "I need feedback on the product I'm building," or "I'm stuck on this technical problem." I tried to figure out ways to not have managers be the answers to those questions. (01:16:48): I'm like, "There should be another answer." And so pair programming really helps you get unblocked quickly because you have another person that you can bounce technical ideas off of. Having a product backlog can tell you what to work on. We had demos every week, demos internally, and then we had demos with the clients every week because we were a contract manufacturing for mobile. That gave them feedback on whether they were going in the right direction. We had set working hours, which made things super intense in the office. This is again like 2009 to 2013. So all these things didn't really need a manager. And what I realized was what the unblocking thing needed a manager. I'm blocked on this. Well, I said, okay, if... I had all these directors. I did two things famously. One, I had a lot of direct reports, and two, I did not do any scheduled one-on-ones because you can't have 120 direct reports and do a scheduled one-on-ones because you're never doing anything but one-on-ones. (01:17:31): So I said, "I'm going to be around a lot because I don't have a lot of one-on-ones. So we can do unscheduled one-on-ones." And what that means is if you are blocked, actually there's a famous picture where I had this weird cube desk where it was like a circle almost in the middle of the whole floor of engineers. And I was always there because I wasn't in a lot of meetings and people that were blocked, they could just come up to me. Actually, one cool thing about pair programming IRL is you can look across and just see if it's working or not. Because if two people are intensely on the computer, you know it's working. If one person is laying back or you're like, "It's not working," so you can just walk up to-
turns.zh: 是啊，最后我们的情况是这样的。一开始只有10个人。我加入XtremeLabs时，不是创始人，但我加入得很早，所有人都向我汇报工作。随着公司发展，我继续让这些人向我汇报，同时我也在思考一个问题——我们谈到“工匠”和“工匠天堂”，即人们不需要经理来解决问题的理念。但我试图用其他方式解决他们依赖经理才能解决的问题。比如，我会问：“我该做什么？”  “产品待办列表卡住了？”  “客户反馈不足？”  “技术难题困住了？” 我试图找到不让经理成为这些问题的唯一解答方式。（01:16:48） 我会说：“应该有其他办法。” 对此，结对编程能快速解锁思路，因为你可以和搭档交流技术问题。产品待办列表能明确工作重点。我们每周内部演示，每周与客户演示（因为我们是移动端外包公司），这样能获得反馈，知道方向是否正确。我们设定固定工作时间，这让办公室氛围非常紧张。这段经历发生在2009至2013年间。这些事务其实不需要经理。但我发现，需要经理的地方在于解除阻塞。比如，遇到卡点时，我会说：“如果……我有这么多下属，我该怎么办。” 我做了两件事：一是增加直属下属数量；二是不安排固定一对一会议，因为120个直属下属不可能每个都单独见面（结果我只能开会）。（01:17:31） 我说：“既然我不常开会，就多在身边待着，这样可以随时解答问题。” 有个著名的照片，展示了我那张奇特的立方体办公桌，几乎占据了整个工程师楼层的中心位置。遇到卡点时，大家总会来找我。现实中，结对编程的妙处在于，你能通过观察了解进展。如果两人专注编码，说明进展顺利；如果一方懈怠，你就知道出问题了。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: It's working if one person is laying back or you're like, it's not working. So you could just walk up to them and be like, "What's happening?" But they would come and ask me questions and I can unlock them. Like, hey, we're blocked on this. We don't have this API. We need money for this machine, whatever. And so the unscheduled one-on-ones ended up being a real clarifying thing for me. Because I did scheduled one-on-ones my whole career and I realized after leaving Microsoft for three years, I'm like, where are all those one-on-ones useful once a week for three years, right? A hundred and fifty one-on-ones. (01:18:26): So the unscheduled ones were, though. I was like, when I knocked on my manager's door and said, "I have this problem, those were important." So that's what I created at Xtreme. And the 120 directors, it just grew over time. I just didn't think I needed managers. So I was like, let me unblock these people on another way. And we came up with other things to systems to unblock them that didn't require a manager. And I just also had a good memory. I knew exactly everyone's skills and compensation. I knew all that off the top of my head, so that helps. (01:18:54): The thing that I broke was actually, this is Chamath. He came in and became our biggest investors. He's obviously is a smart guy, but he said the right thing, which is not, this can never work, because then I would go into defense mode and explain to him why it would work. He just said to me, I'm not going to debate with you whether this works or not, but will it work at 400 people? And I said, probably not. He said, okay, so let's change it. (01:19:16): And so we did then ended up putting a little bit more of a structure, but I made a few people directors and I forced them to have 40 direct reports each. I said, we're just going to make it still pretty flat. And then that did end up working, because it still allowed them to use the system to unblock people versus having to do a one-on-one every week, or having to talk about things that potentially a system could unblock. And so I tried to figure out ways to systematize things.
turns.zh: 只要有一个人在休息，或者你觉得“这行不通”，那就去找他们，问他们：“怎么回事？”但他们可能会来问我问题，而我能帮他们解决。比如，“我们遇到了这个技术难题。没有这项API。我们需要钱买这台机器等等。” 所以这些非计划性的单独交流对我来说很有启发意义。因为我整个职业生涯都在参加定期的一对一会议，但离开微软三年后，我才意识到，三年来每周一次的定期一对一会议到底有什么用呢？总共参加了150次一对一会议。（01:18:26）不过非计划性的交流确实有效。比如，我敲开经理的办公室门说：“我遇到这个问题了”，结果这些交流很重要。这就是我在Xtreme公司推行的机制。120个主管职位也是随着时间自然增长的。我觉得自己不需要经理，所以想用其他方式帮他们解除阻碍。我们开发了不需要经理参与的解除阻碍系统，而且我记忆力很好，对每个人的技能和薪资都了如指掌，这很有帮助。（01:18:54）我搞砸的部分是Chamath。他加入后成为我们最大的投资者。他显然很聪明，但他说了正确的话，不是说“这永远行不通”，因为那样我会进入防御模式，解释为什么行得通。他只对我说：我不想和你争论这是否可行，但400人规模能行吗？我说可能不行。他说：那就改吧。（01:19:16）于是我们增加了些结构化流程，让一些人成为主管，每人负责40个直接下属。我们决定保持组织结构尽可能扁平化。结果确实奏效了，因为员工仍能通过系统解除阻碍，而不必每周进行一对一沟通，或是去处理本可以通过系统解决的问题。所以我一直在探索如何将事务系统化。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. Just another example of doing things differently, not necessarily just, here's how it's done and I'm going to do it that way and experimenting with it. Even if you knew, okay, maybe long term this isn't the way it's going to operate. I imagine at Shopify you don't have 120 reports.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这样。这又是一个以不同方式做事的例子，不一定是那种“这就是标准做法，我要照搬”的做法，而是去尝试、去实验。即便你知道，或许从长远看这行不通。我猜Shopify没有120个下属吧。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: No, we have fourteen or something. We do have these guardrails where I think we say, Hey, in engineering you should have between eight and 20. There are definitely people who have more and people who have less. But we do try to keep things as flat as possible, because we do believe that it doesn't make sense to have three people reporting to and then to somebody, and then they only have three people. You just make a very deep hierarchy. We actually do see, by the way, the farther you are from Toby, we can see things in the survey results. The alignment gets out of whack, and so you do actually see that you want to be closer, you want to have a flatter org in general, and that can be achieved by just having more direct reports per level.
turns.zh: 没有，我们有14个左右。我们确实有一些基本规则，比如在工程部门，8到20个下属比较合适。当然有些人下属更多，有些人更少。但我们确实尽可能保持扁平化结构，因为我们认为三层级结构没意义，上面三个人管下面一个人，然后下面三个人又管下面一个人。这样就会形成很深的层级结构。顺便说一句，从Toby这里越远的员工，调查结果越差。组织一致性越差，所以你确实能看出，大家都希望更贴近高层，希望组织更扁平化，而这可以通过增加每个层级的直接下属数量来实现。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Makes sense. Okay, final question before we get to our very exciting lightning round. We have this recurring segments that I call Fail Corner where generally people come on these podcasts, they share all their successes. Here's all the things that I've done, right. Here's all the big wins. And everyone feels like, oh man, I wish I was always successful people. When in reality, everyone that comes on has failed many times. Is there a story of a failure in your career that you could share that helps people see that even folks like you fail, and maybe what you learned from that experience?
turns.zh: 挺有道理的。好的，在进入我们非常激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，最后一个问题。我们有这样一个固定环节，我称之为“失败角”，在这个环节中，嘉宾们通常会分享他们的成功故事。比如“我做过这些事”，“我取得了这些重大成就”。大家都会感叹“天哪，我真希望自己也能一直成功”。但现实是，每位嘉宾都经历过多次失败。您能否分享自己职业生涯中的一次失败经历，让大家明白即使像您这样的人也会遭遇挫折，并从中汲取教训呢？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: I have a few. I'll say one thing by the way, because I think I read this in Tim Ferriss's book or in the podcast where he said, create a failure resume and write everything down. And I would not recommend doing this because I did this and I got super... I'm like a high energy happy guy. I wrote down, I have a note on my phone called Failure Resume, and I wrote down all the times I failed and it is depressing. So I would not encourage people to do that, but I'm happy to tell you about a few instances. (01:21:33): So well, one is actually I've been laid off twice and people would not expect like, oh, I'm doing this thing and I've been laid off twice. And I think in both times it was the right thing, it was the right thing for the company, the right thing for me. (01:21:45): And I kind of used that experience as a way to reevaluate and eventually came out with my framework of how I want to spend time. But that's maybe a different story. (01:21:54): I'll tell you about one at Shopify, the first week that I started, 2019, we were rebuilding our point of sale system, which now does billions of dollars of GMB. But back then we were like, well, let's rebuild it with a new UX and a new technology platform. And it was my first week and I'm the mobile guy, coming from Extreme Labs. They're like, should we build this in React Native, or should we build this natively on the mobile platforms? And so I went through this evaluation, spent a lot of time, blah, blah, blah, and I came back with a hedged solution, which is kind of dumb. I said, let's do iOS and Swift and let's do Android in React Native. And the reason I said that was I said, I want to learn about React Native and I think Android's the harder platform, so let's build that in React Native, but iOS on Swift because that guarantees us a product in market. And we didn't have any React Native apps in market at the time. A year later we launched the iOS version and it was a huge success. And we then spent another six months building the React Native version for Android and everything else. And we realized pretty quickly that React Native was the platform for the future. We were like, oh my God, this will allow us to have one platform. You could run it on the web as well, and we could use the React engineers from the web to work on it. It was a clear winner. By then, we had also launched a shop app, which is React Native. (01:23:11): And so we learned a lot about this. And I went back and I said, hey everybody, I made a huge mistake. We just spent a year building this thing. It's in market, but we're going to have to rewrite. We're going to have to rebase back onto this iOS version. And I think I burned 18 months of time with a hundred engineers, literally from the decision I made in the first week of joining Shopify, and Toby, when I went to Toby and I told him, I go, hey man, I think I made this mistake and we have to do this and it's going to cost us a hundred engineers, another six, whatever. And he looked at me and he goes, you should tell everyone this story. That's all he said. Not like, hey, bad, good. He goes, did you learn something? It was an epiphany for me, but he was like, this is a learning org, and I totally failed and I told everyone I failed and my mistake and everything else, but he goes, just tell everyone because he goes, do you know what mistake you made? (01:23:57): And first I was like, I don't think, like, what mistake. He's like, you didn't take. He goes, I will always come down harshly on people who do not take risks, and you did not take a risk in this case. But if you take a risk and it doesn't work out, you'll never get in trouble, because you took the risk and it was the right risk to take, but he goes, but you didn't take the risk. (01:24:16): And so what I should have done, and by the way, even now thinking back it would be super hard to do, first week at Shopify, right, is take a risk on a platform that we have not launched in production app on, but he was correct in that we should have, because we would've saved ourselves so much more time. So yeah, total failure, sorry. The product is super successful now and we're all on React Native and even the Shop Green app is on React Native. Everything's React Native, and we're core contributors. It's all good. But I literally burned I think 18 months of time for a hundred engineers as my first decision in the company.
turns.zh:
我有过几次失败的经历。顺便说一句，我记得在蒂姆·费里斯（Tim Ferriss）的书或播客中看到过一个建议，叫做“制作一份失败履历表”，把所有失败经历都写下来。但我不建议这么做，因为我自己试过，结果非常糟糕。我本来是个精力充沛、乐观开朗的人，但写下那些失败经历后，真的很压抑。所以我不建议大家这么做，但我可以分享几个例子。（01:21:33）：比如说，我被裁过两次。人们可能觉得奇怪，哦，我才刚加入公司就被裁两次。但我觉得两次裁员都是正确的决定，对公司和个人来说都是最好的选择。（01:21:45）：我把这段经历当作重新审视自我的契机，最终形成了我理想的生活框架。不过这或许是另一个故事了。（01:21:54）：说说Shopify的经历吧。2019年我刚加入公司的第一周，我们就着手重建当时价值数十亿美元的GMB（全球商户平台）的销售点系统。但当时我们面临一个技术挑战——是用React Native还是原生平台来开发？作为移动部门的负责人，我需要做出选择。团队问我：是用React Native还是原生平台？于是我经过深思熟虑，最终提出了一个折中方案：iOS用Swift，Android用React Native。原因是我想学习React Native，又觉得Android平台更难，所以选择在iOS上用Swift开发，而Android用React Native。但一年后我们发布iOS版本时，取得了巨大成功。之后又花了六个月为Android开发React Native版本，结果发现React Native才是未来的趋势。我们意识到，未来可以将一个平台适配到网页端，利用Web端的React工程师共同开发。这是一个完美的解决方案。当时我们还推出了React Native版本的Shopify应用。（01:23:11）：从中我们吸取了宝贵教训。我回去跟团队说：我犯了个大错，浪费了一年时间。虽然产品上线了，但我们必须重写代码，回退到iOS版本。当时我动用了100名工程师，耗费了18个月的时间。这全都源于我加入Shopify第一周做的那个决定。后来我去找托比（Toby）说，我觉得自己犯了错，必须重写代码，回退到iOS版本。他只说了一句：你应该把这个故事分享给所有人。没有批评，也没有安慰。他问：你从中学到了什么？这对我来说是个顿悟。他说Shopify是个学习型组织，我坦诚承认错误，分享教训，但他强调：你要把错误公开，让大家引以为戒。（01:23:57）：起初我很困惑，觉得自己哪里错了。他说：你没有冒险精神。他说：我对不肯冒险的人零容忍，而你这次就是缺乏冒险精神。但如果
即便你冒了风险却没成功，也绝不会因此陷入困境，因为你当初的冒险是明智之举。但他却说，你根本没冒险。（01:24:16）所以我本该怎么做呢？说实话，即便现在回想起来也知道这很难做到——毕竟那是我加入Shopify的第一周。当时我们应该在一个尚未投入生产的平台上冒险尝试，但他说得没错，我们确实应该这么做，因为这样能为我们节省大量时间。好吧，那次尝试确实彻底失败了，很抱歉。不过现在这个产品非常成功，我们全公司都采用了React Native，甚至Shop Green应用也迁移到了React Native。所有产品都用上了React Native，我们还是核心贡献者。这结果还是不错的。但我记得，我在公司做出的第一个决策，直接让100名工程师白白浪费了18个月的时间。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This might be the best example of failure coordinator we've had yet. This is a great example. Both of them actually are, although I'm wondering, okay, that felt like a really good decision to me and it's-
turns.zh: 这或许是我们遇到过的最典型的失败协调者案例了。这确实是个绝佳的例子。说实话，他们俩都属于这种类型，不过我还是想说，嗯，我当时觉得这真是个很明智的决策——

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: It sounds like it, right? But It wouldn't have been his.
turns.zh: 听起来确实如此，对吧？但那本不该是他的选择。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But it's, obviously you don't want to just take risks. There's a limit of a risk but informed, I guess. Is there anything you missed there that would told you this was the right path? Because in hindsight, of course we should have done this, but looking back, what do you think you should have done other than we should have done the risky path?
turns.zh: 但显然，你不想只是一味地冒险。风险固然有其限度，但必须是明智的冒险。你们有没有遗漏什么关键信息，导致你们认为这条路是正确的？因为事后看来，我们当然应该这么做，但回头看，你们觉得除了选择冒险路径，还有什么别的做法呢？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, I mean one thing about my career as well is I don't really do anything halfway. And when I started looking into React Native, it was never just that I'm going, oh, let me look at the docs and read and build a thing. It's like I flew to Meta and met with the React team. I became a core contributor. I ran the React Native working group, like we became release captains for React Native. I knew that I was going to do all the things, so I'm like, and of course in React Native you can also drop down to native and do things there that are not possible. So I think I hedged incorrectly. I knew I was going to do all these things and I should have looked at my own thought process, say, if I do all the things, can I fail? And I didn't take that into account because again, I did five or six. (01:25:58): I literally, I put everyone together. I was running the group, I was like release captain. I would hang out with the React team and Meta, we're doing all the things. We became core contributors at React Native before we became core contributors and react because of all the things I was doing. And so I think just knowing that I was going to go all out, I should have said, you know what? This is not going to fail. And I didn't have the confidence in that path, so I hedged, right? Hedging is the worst. And I remember the CTO at the time said, I'm wondering if I should force you to go React Native. He literally said that. And I said, I will do if you say that, I will do it, but it would've been his decision. And so he didn't do it. He didn't tell me to do it.
turns.zh: 是啊，我职业生涯的一个特点就是从不半途而废。当我开始研究 React Native 时，绝不是随便看看文档、读读代码然后搭建个东西那么简单。我飞到 Meta 公司，与 React 团队会面。我成了核心贡献者，负责 React Native 工作组的运营。我们甚至成为 React Native 版本发布的负责人。当时我就知道自己必须全力以赴，所以我总在想，如果我把所有事情都做好了，还能失败吗？但我没考虑到这一点，因为我确实做了五六件事。（01:25:58）我简直把所有人都召集起来了。我领导着这个团队，担任发布负责人，与 React 团队和 Meta 公司密切合作。我们因投入的巨大精力而成为 React Native 的核心贡献者，甚至早于成为 React 的核心贡献者。所以我觉得既然决定全力以赴，就应该坚定信心说，这条路绝不会失败。但我对这条路线缺乏信心，所以选择了退缩，对吧？退缩是最糟糕的选择。我记得当时的首席技术官曾说，想强制我采用 React Native。他真的这么说了。我回答，如果你这么做，我会照做，但那将是他的决定。他最终没有这么做，也没有命令我这么做。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, that makes a lot more sense. It's so funny that Facebook had a similar mistake early on in their career-
turns.zh: 好吧，这下更说得通了。真有趣的是，Facebook 在早期也犯过类似的错误——

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: HTML5.
turns.zh: HTML5。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly. I know. I don't know if you were at Zuck's interview at the Chase center that the Acquired podcast did, and he talked about this where their market cap dropped 80%. They were about to go public. They went with this app. No one thought they could do mobile ads. And he's like, that set us back a year and a half. He's like, but based on all the pain he's gone through back since then, he's like, that was not too bad.
turns.zh: 是啊，确实如此。我知道。你可能听过 Acquired 播客在 Chase 中心对扎克伯格的采访，他谈到过那个事件，当时他们的市值暴跌 80%，眼看就要上市了，结果推出了那个应用。当时没人认为他们能做移动广告。他说，嗯，那让我们倒退了一年半。但基于后来经历的种种挫折，他觉得那也不算太糟。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, it's true actually, maybe what people don't know is, I was at Facebook, XtremeLabs, worked on the Facebook app and we worked on that app. I was in the office when we submitted the iOS app every single day that week, because it kept crashing. And we had obviously direct access to people at Apple, but we'd ship a new app on Monday and it crashed ship an app on... Not just us, but us, Facebook together. And so I remember that whole HTML five fiasco from the inside.
turns.zh: 是啊，说实话，人们可能不知道的是，我曾在 Facebook 的 XtremeLabs 工作，参与过 Facebook 应用的开发。记得那周我们每天都在办公室提交 iOS 应用版本，因为它老是崩溃。当时我们显然能直接接触到苹果公司的人，但周一刚发布新应用，周三就崩溃了。不只是我们，Facebook 整个团队都遇到了这个问题。因此，我从内部视角见证了整个 HTML5 事件的全过程。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I thought you would say you also told Facebook to decide on the HTML5 app to set them back a year.
turns.zh: 我以为你会说你还让Facebook决定采用HTML5应用，让他们倒退一年。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: I did not. We happened to be there when they were doing it. Yeah.
turns.zh: 我没有。我们碰巧在他们做这件事的时候在场。是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's so funny. Amazing. Thank you for sharing that. Before we get to a very exciting lightning round, is there anything else that you think would be valuable to leave listeners with, either touch on something you've mentioned, a last piece of nugget of wisdom, or we just go straight to the round?
turns.zh: 太有趣了。太棒了。谢谢你分享这个。在我们进入非常激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你觉得还有什么对听众有价值的信息可以留下，或者是提及你之前提到过的东西，或者是一个最后的智慧金句，或者我们直接进入问答环节？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, I'll say something maybe embarrassing for you. I've been using your performance management framework from your first round review article, not knowing by the way that it was you. I actually found it, you being the famous Lenny podcaster, but the old days, maybe the Lenny, the PM. And I remember reading this a long time ago and just copying, there's a Google link in there to a Google Doc link with a template for a performance review framework that I've been using for years. (01:28:32): Literally every review I've done at Shopify uses that framework. And I was writing a post to my admin about how we can use LLMs to make it easier for me to write these reviews, even though obviously you have to read it all and go through it, but I was like, how can I generate some of this with an LLM? And so I wanted to send her the original article. So I went back to the first round review, I found the article and said, oh my God, it's Lenny, the same guy. (01:28:54): So I will say one thing that's interesting about that framework is, I've used it now for, like I said, six years here, is that, and I don't think it's me. I think it's actually the framework pulls out good information. I've had multiple people in a review process tell me that, when I deliver the feedback in, of course the format, they would say, wow, I've been in industry a long time. This is the best performance review I've ever had. And it's because the framework pulls out good information. So congrats to you. (01:29:21): But I think it was funny that randomly I was coming on this podcast and I just wrote that doc to my admin two, three weeks ago and realized it's the same person.
turns.zh: 是的，我要说一些可能会让你尴尬的事。我一直在使用你第一轮评审文章中的绩效管理框架，却不知道那是你写的。实际上，我是在旧金山工作时发现它的，当时你还是著名的播客主Lenny，但在过去的日子里，也许你还是那个PM Lenny。我记得很久以前读到这篇文章，就直接复制了下来，里面有一个Google链接，指向一个Google Doc模板，我已经用了好几年了。（01:28:32）：我在Shopify做的每一次评审都用了这个框架。我还写了一篇帖子给我的行政助理，讲如何用LLM让评审更轻松，尽管显然你还是需要通读并审核，但我想，如何用LLM生成部分内容呢？所以我想把原文发给她。于是我回顾了第一轮评审，找到了那篇文章，天哪，原来是Lenny，同一个人啊。（01:28:54）：所以关于这个框架的一个有趣之处是，我在这里用了六年，现在看来，不是我的问题，而是框架本身能提取出有用的信息。很多参与评审的人都告诉我，当我给出反馈时，尽管格式一样，他们还是会说，哇，我在行业里这么久了，这是我经历过的最好的绩效评审。这是因为框架能提取出有用的信息。所以恭喜你了。（01:29:21）：但有趣的是，我偶然来听这个播客，两三周前刚把那份文档发给我的行政助理，结果发现是同一个人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, how about that? I love that. I'll also give credit to a four board guest on this podcast, Vlad Loktev, who was my manager at Airbnb, and that's where I was inspired to write about that framework.
turns.zh: 哇，真是巧合。我太喜欢这个了。我还要感谢这个播客的第四期嘉宾Vlad Loktev，他曾是我在Airbnb的经理，我就是从他那里获得了灵感写下那个框架。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it trickles down to him and I don't know where he boarded this, he probably invented it. So credit to Vlad also for that. Another fun fact along these lines, I have another first round of repost about the W framework, which is a framework for planning. They do annual planning. And that's one that I've slowly discovered many, many companies use and they don't know where it came from. They just call it, oh, we have this W framework. Someone flipped it and call the M framework. But that's another one that has trickled into the ether of tech companies, which is awesome.
turns.zh: 所以这个框架慢慢传播开来，我都不知道它从哪里来的，可能Vlad自己发明的。所以也要感谢Vlad。另一个有趣的事实是，我还有另一篇关于W框架的第一轮转载文章，W框架是一个用于规划的框架。他们每年做规划。我慢慢发现很多公司都在用这个框架，却不知道它从哪里来的。他们只称之为W框架，有人把它改名叫M框架。但这又是一个慢慢渗透进科技公司圈子的框架，真是太棒了。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: With that, Farhan, we have reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 好的，Farhan，我们进入令人兴奋的闪电问答环节了。你准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 我准备好了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's do this. What are two or three books that you have recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 咱们开始吧。你最近向别人推荐得最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: There's one. So Toby has an annoyingly long set of books that he recommends, and they're all, not all, they're usually good, depends because we're not totally in sync on fiction, for example. But he recommended one to me that I think everyone should read right now called Manna, M-A-N-N-A, from Marshall Brain. It is a book, it's a book about AI. And I think the most interesting thing about it though is about a future in which the AI tells the humans what to do. So it's this idea of, imagine in the future you came into work and the AI would tell you what emails to pay attention to or what dashboard to look at because something weird is going on. It takes that to an interesting level. So I would recommend reading that book. It's not long. That's fun. (01:31:05): I think another book that I recommend to people, and it's a weird one to recommend, but it's Business Adventures from John Brooks, the famous, if you ask, I think it's Bill Gates, what his famous book of all time is, it's this book. (01:31:16): And the cool thing about the book is that it is not easy to digest for anyone with focus problems. Paul Graham wrote the post How to Do Great Work, and it's super long. The best part about that post is that you have to be able to read the whole thing. And so the same thing with Business Adventures. I think each chapter is, it's 12 chapters, 12 stories, no breaks in between. It's just each one is super long. But it just goes into a problem at such depth that if you can maintain your focus to get through the depths of each problem, you will just learn something, just like that post by Paul Graham. (01:31:51): I loved that it was so long because I sent it to people and I said, the test here is can you read it? Can you just get to the end? And not in a pejorative way, like in a... If you can get to the end, you will extract the alpha from this post if you can read it all. So those are... Manna is like the opposite. It's very easy and easy read.
turns.zh: 就一本吧。托比推荐的书多得让人头疼，但也确实不错，不过我们在小说方面的品味不太一致。比如，他推荐给我的一本叫《Manna》的书，作者是马歇尔·布莱恩，讲的是人工智能的。最有趣的点在于，书中设想未来人工智能会告诉人类该做什么。比如你去上班，人工智能会提醒你关注哪些邮件，或者查看哪些仪表盘，因为系统发现了异常情况。这部分设想很吸引人。所以我推荐大家读这本书。书不算长，很有趣。（01:31:05）：我还推荐过一本奇怪的书，是约翰·布鲁克斯的《商业冒险》。要问谁推荐的书最多，我觉得是比尔·盖茨。他说自己最喜欢的书就是这本。（01:31:16）：这本书的妙处在于，注意力不集中的读者很难读下去。保罗·格雷厄姆写过《如何做好工作》那篇长文，同样需要专注力。这本书也是如此，每章都是12个故事，没有分隔符，每个故事都超长。但正因如此，它对每个问题的剖析极其深入。只要你能保持专注，钻研每个问题的深层逻辑，就能收获知识，就像保罗·格雷厄姆那篇长文一样。（01:31:51）：我喜欢它篇幅长，因为我把它推荐给别人时说：考验就在于你能否读完。能读完就说明你能从中汲取精华。《Manna》则相反，读起来很轻松。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm excited to read these. Next question. Do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show you really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 我很期待读这些书。下一个问题。你最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: A recent one was Challengers, the tennis movie, with Zendaya just randomly I was at home and I put it on and the cool thing about it was more the cinematography and music. They had this weird style, art house style, where they would be talking and music would get super loud. It was very strange, but a very, very good movie. And then you saw, you said movies and-
turns.zh: 最近看的《挑战者》这部网球题材电影挺不错的，主演是赞达亚。我在家随手点开看的，最棒的是摄影和音乐。他们用一种很奇特的艺术风格，拍对话时音乐会突然变得很大，很怪异，但确实是部好电影。然后你提到电影和——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Or TV show. Oh, TV show, anything like that.
turns.zh: 电视剧。哦，电视剧啊，随便说点。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yeah, one of my all time favorites is probably Halt and Catch Fire. I don't know if you've watched that.
turns.zh: 对，我最喜欢的剧之一是《编辑部喜事》，不知道你看过没。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: About the early tech industry.
turns.zh: 讲早期科技行业的。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Early tech. And I think there was an Andreessen podcast where he said this is the closest thing to what a real startup looks like. So Halt and Catch Fire like an all time recommend, everybody has to watch it.
turns.zh: 早期科技。安德森在播客里说这是最接近真实创业公司的作品。所以《编辑部喜事》绝对值得推荐，每个人都该看看。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite product that you recently discovered that you really love?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现什么特别喜欢的产品？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: I don't know if I want to be in the zeitgeist right now, but the Meta Ray-Bans are amazing. And the biggest thing about the Meta Ray-Bans was just that I think I never got into it and I saw people around me wearing it, but I only got into it when somebody said I'd never take my AirPods with me anymore. And I was like, oh, I can swap two devices for one device. I always have sunglasses and AirPods because I'll go for a walk or listen to a podcast and now I can just have one device. (01:33:26): And this happened to me. I was in the summer, I was at a pool party and someone called me and I just took it from my sunglasses and people were confused as where I was taking this call from. But they are the right amount of tech. They're in unintrusive, you can't tell, they don't look like any tech. And then also I was playing soccer with my kids. I have three kids. I just turned the video on and I was the goalie and they were taking shots and I was watching them. They had no idea that I was just recording. And it was such a cool moment because I was in playing soccer with them. I wasn't with my phone and I got to get this amazing set of video that I would never would've gotten. So I really liked the Meta Ray-Bans.
turns.zh: 我不知道自己现在是否想紧跟时代潮流，但Meta Ray-Bans真是太棒了。而Meta Ray-Bans最吸引我的地方在于，我之前从未真正关注过这款产品，但看到身边的人戴着它时，我才意识到它的魅力。直到有人说我再也不用随身携带AirPods了，我才真正入了坑。我当时想，哦，我可以用一台设备替代两件物品。我总会随身携带太阳镜和AirPods——无论是去散步还是听播客，现在只需携带一台设备就够了。（01:33:26）：这种情况在我身上也发生过。那年夏天，我在泳池派对上接到电话，直接从太阳镜上取下手机，周围的人都好奇我从哪儿接的电话。但它们恰到好处地融入了科技元素，既不显眼，又不像传统科技产品。还有一次我带孩子们踢足球。我有三个孩子。我打开视频录制，自己当守门员，孩子们不断射门，而我全程在观察。他们完全不知道我在拍摄。这真是个很棒的时刻，因为我能和孩子们一起踢球，不用掏出手机，还能拍下这些珍贵的画面。我真的很喜欢Meta Ray-Bans。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We had Boz on the podcast who leads a lot of that work and he's got a to teach us. And I put on Ray-Bans while we were doing the interview just for fun. You could see my setup. Okay, cool. Two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you find useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 我们节目请到了Boz，他负责大部分相关工作，他能教会我们很多东西。采访时我戴上Ray-Bans只是为了好玩。大家可以看看我的设备设置。好的，再问两个问题。你有没有一条在工作或生活中觉得很有用的座右铭？

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Okay, I do. And it's on a lot of my profile bios, and it is, everything you know is wrong. And the reason I like that one, and people always like, what would you put on a billboard? And people always come back to me and say, that's like they know that as my motto. (01:34:32): And the reason for that is it's this notion of if all the knowledge you knew was incorrect, could you from first principles build up a view of the world? And that's kind of how I like to think of things is that, anything could be incorrect. Even things that you think are correct, which is why, again, back to the, I like to experiment. I like to look stupid, because I'm always trying shit because I'm like, I don't know if even though you say this is correct, that this is going to work, right. (01:34:58): Actually, one example, my wife hates this is I have a Tesla and I routinely will switch gears without fully stopping the car, which you cannot do in a regular car, but I'll be in drive and then I'll slow down to drive back up into my driveway and while it's moving I switch it into reverse. (01:35:14): And you never would know that that's possible except for trying. And sometimes it goes beep beep because you're going too fast. And she hates it. But I'm always trying weird things and so that's why I say everything you know is wrong. Who knows what's possible, just try different things.
turns.zh: 有的。这句话经常出现在我的个人简介里：你所知道的一切都是错的。我喜欢这句话的原因是，它启发我思考：如果现有知识都是错误的，能否从第一性原理出发重建世界观？这也是我思考问题的方式——任何事都可能是错的，即便你认为正确的事也可能出错。这也是我喜欢尝试新事物的原因。我愿意看起来像个傻瓜，因为我总在不断尝试。比如，我妻子讨厌我开特斯拉时不停车就换挡，这在普通车上是不允许的，但我会在行驶中切换到倒挡。（01:34:58）：除非亲自尝试，否则你永远不会知道这能行得通。有时还会因为车速过快而听到提示音。她特别讨厌我这样做。但我总在尝试新奇的事物，所以我才会说你所知道的一切都是错的。谁知道未来会有什么可能，勇敢尝试吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I do the same thing with my Tesla. I used to do it with a non-electric car and my wife is always like, don't do that. Screwing it up.
turns.zh: 我也用特斯拉这么做过。我以前开非电动车时也这样，我妻子总是说别这样，会把车弄坏的。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yes, exactly.
turns.zh: 是啊，没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that on an electric car, there's no gear you're breaking, it's just software.
turns.zh: 我喜欢电动车没有变速箱的问题，全靠软件控制。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This quote reminds me of that you shared of everything you know is wrong. The founders of Airbnb always talked about just this point that everything around you was designed somebody, another human. There's not necessarily that much smarter or insightful. It doesn't mean what they did was correct. Somebody else find some better potentially...
turns.zh: 这段引言让我想起你分享过的，关于你知道的所有错误之处的故事。Airbnb的创始人总是强调这一点——你周围的一切都是由人设计的，并非必然更聪明或更有洞察力。这并不意味着他们做得对，别人总能找到更好的方案。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: I think Steve Jobs had a similar thing like, hey, you can design anything. Everything's designed by people. I love that one too.
turns.zh: 我觉得史蒂夫·乔布斯也有类似的观点，他曾说过，你可以设计任何东西。一切都是由人设计的。我也很喜欢这句话。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. Final question. So you told me the story of this PhD you hired versus just a guy you met in a college, sorry, in a coffee shop. I read another similar story where you hired a waitress.
turns.zh: 是的。最后一个问题。你之前给我讲过你雇用博士生和在咖啡店遇到的普通人的故事。我还读到过另一个类似的故事，说你雇用了一位女服务员。

turns.speaker: Farhan Thawar
turns.en: Yes.
